stories.title: These Gardeners Have Reused Their Household Items to Grow Plants: 7 Things You Can Use Too
stories.summary: A healthy garden does not always require expensive pots, planters, or gardening equipment. Some of the things that can help plants grow may already be sitting in your kitchen or storeroom, waiting to be thrown away. From plastic bottles and old buckets to kitchen scraps and eggshells, everyday household items can find a second life in a garden. Indian gardeners are already putting these ideas into practice, turning discarded materials into growing spaces and organic compost. Here are seven ways to reuse household items in your garden, inspired by people who are doing it themselves. 1. Plastic bottles can become planters Empty plastic bottles can be turned into planters for herbs, leafy greens, and other plants that do not need much root space. Wash a bottle thoroughly, cut it to the desired size, and make drainage holes at the bottom before adding potting mix.   A healthy garden does not always require expensive pots, planters, or gardening equipment. Photograph: (OneGreenPlanet) You can also arrange bottles vertically to make use of a small balcony wall. Mandeep Sangwan and students in Delhi created vertical gardens using discarded plastic bottles. Their initiative shows how waste can be turned into green spaces, even where ground space is limited.  2. Old buckets and containers can grow vegetables An unused bucket, plastic tub, or drum can provide a home for tomatoes, chillies, and leafy greens. Choose a container that is deep enough for the crop, clean it thoroughly, and make drainage holes before filling it with potting mix. Avoid containers that previously held paint, pesticides, oils, or other chemicals, especially when growing edible plants. Shivanand Hongal and students in Sirsi, Karnataka , found creative ways to reuse waste in their garden. Along with plastic bottles, they used broken buckets, cement bags, and tin cans to grow plants. Their work shows how discarded objects can become practical growing containers.  3. Coconut shells can become small planters Coconut shells are sturdy and can be used as small planters for succulents, seedlings, and other compact plants. Clean the shell, make drainage holes if possible, and fill it with a suitable potting mix. They can also add a natural touch to a balcony garden. However, their limited size makes them unsuitable for plants that need plenty of room for their roots. Sakshi Bharadwaj from Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh , has reused materials such as coconut shells and plastic bottles in her garden, which features thousands of plants. Her approach offers inspiration for gardeners who want to make use of everyday discarded objects.  4. Vegetable peels can become compost Fruit peels, vegetable scraps, and other suitable kitchen waste can be turned into compost. Instead of throwing away banana peels, carrot tops, and other uncooked scraps, collect them in a home compost bin. Mix these green materials with brown materials such as dry leaves, shredded cardboard, and uncoated paper. Keep the mixture moist but not waterlogged, and turn it occasionally to allow air to circulate.   Fruit peels, vegetable scraps, and other suitable kitchen waste can be turned into compost. K Subbalakshmi from Vijayawada, Andhra Pradesh , uses household wet waste to make compost for her garden. Her example shows how kitchen waste can be put to use instead of being sent to landfill. Avoid adding meat, dairy products, and oils to a basic home compost pile, as these can attract pests and create unpleasant odours. 5. Eggshells can be added to compost Eggshells contain calcium carbonate and can be added to a home compost pile. Rinse them, allow them to dry, and crush them into small pieces before mixing them with vegetable scraps and dry leaves. Crushing the shells helps them break down more readily, although decomposition can still take time. Eggshells are not an instant fertiliser, so do not rely on them alone to address a plant’s nutritional needs. Evangeline Wilson from Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh , has worked to reduce household waste by composting kitchen scraps and making use of materials such as eggshells, tea leaves, and vegetable peels.  6. Used tea leaves can enrich compost After making chai , save the used tea leaves rather than throwing them away. They can be added to compost, where they contribute organic matter as they decompose. Let the leaves cool before collecting them and mix them with dry leaves, cardboard, or other brown materials. If you use tea bags, check whether they contain plastic and remove any non-compostable parts. Tea leaves can be useful compost ingredients, but they should not replace a balanced compost mix. Avoid piling large quantities directly around plant stems. Evangeline Wilson’s waste-reduction efforts in Prayagraj also offer a useful example of how everyday kitchen leftovers can be diverted from the rubbish bin and put to better use.  7. Newspapers and cardboard can help suppress weeds Plain cardboard and uncoated newspapers can help cover bare soil and suppress weeds around established plants. Remove tape, staples, and plastic labels before using them.   Reusing household items does not mean saving everything that might possibly be useful. Photograph: (Etsy) Lay the cardboard over the soil, leaving space around plant stems, and wet it so that it stays in place. Cover it with dry leaves or another suitable organic mulch. Shredded newspaper can also be added to compost as a source of carbon. Avoid glossy paper and cardboard contaminated with grease or chemicals. Do not pack cardboard tightly against plant stems, as this can trap moisture and encourage rot. This is another way to reduce household waste while making garden maintenance easier. If you have old packaging or newspapers, check whether they are suitable for reuse before putting them in the bin. Make the most of what you have Reusing household items does not mean saving everything that might possibly be useful. The key is to choose materials that are clean, safe, and suitable for the task. Start with one or two ideas that suit your home and the plants you already grow. A few simple changes can reduce waste while making gardening more affordable. Sometimes, the next useful addition to your garden is already waiting in your kitchen or storeroom.

stories.title: Why Bihar Museum Ranks 9th in the World, Beating New York’s Met & Other Icons
stories.summary: What makes a museum worth travelling across the world for? In Patna, Bihar Museum has made a strong case for itself. It has been ranked ninth among the world’s 100 best museums in 2026, ahead of New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, popularly known as The Met, and Paris’s Louvre. Designed by Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki, Bihar Museum brings contemporary architecture and the state’s rich cultural heritage together. Photograph: (Instagram/ @just.adulting ) Worth a Journey, an independent travel guide based in Munich, Germany, compiled the ranking using visitor reviews, data analysis, and on-site assessments. Bihar Museum is the highest-ranked museum in Asia on its list and the only Indian institution to feature in the top 100. But beyond the ranking, what can visitors expect to find here? Think ancient sculptures, archaeological treasures, folk art and contemporary architecture, all coming together to tell the story of a region whose cultural legacy stretches back centuries. A modern space for Bihar’s ancient stories Established in 2015, Bihar Museum was created to give the state’s rich collection of historical artefacts a larger space for display. The existing Patna Museum already held a substantial collection, but a new institution offered an opportunity to present Bihar’s heritage on a much larger scale. Spread across more than 13 acres, the museum was designed by Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki, in collaboration with Mumbai-based Opolis Architects. The result is a contemporary building with expansive galleries, open courtyards and landscaped spaces that make exploring the museum an experience in itself. Ancient sculptures at Bihar Museum offer a glimpse into Bihar’s artistic traditions and centuries-old history. Photograph: (Instagram/ @patnaite ) Inside, the exhibits take visitors through Bihar’s history, from its early civilisations to 1764. Ancient sculptures, archaeological finds, coins and manuscripts offer glimpses into the lives, beliefs and artistic traditions of people who lived here long before the modern state took shape. The museum also makes room for living traditions, with galleries dedicated to folk and contemporary art. Together, the collections tell a story that goes beyond dynasties and dates to explore how people have expressed themselves through art and culture . What makes it worth the journey? For families travelling with children, the museum has a dedicated Children’s Gallery featuring subjects such as animals, folk art, culture and science. It offers younger visitors a way to engage with the exhibits beyond simply looking at objects behind glass. The Diaspora Gallery explores Bihar’s connections with communities beyond the state, adding another dimension to its history. And for visitors who want to sample local flavours along the way, the museum also has a restaurant serving Bihari cuisine. Bihar Museum’s folk art collections celebrate the artistic traditions that continue to shape the state’s cultural identity. Photograph: ( NewsMobile ) The architecture is another reason to spend time here. The interplay of indoor galleries, open spaces and landscaped courtyards gives visitors room to pause between exhibits. Rather than treating history as a collection of artefacts to hurry past, the museum offers several ways to explore it at one's own pace. For anyone visiting Patna , it is an opportunity to discover Bihar through its art, people and past, all under one roof. The company Bihar Museum keeps Bihar Museum’s ninth-place ranking puts it among some of the world’s best-known cultural institutions. Mexico City’s Museo Nacional de Antropología leads the 2026 list, followed by Madrid’s Museo del Prado and Denmark’s Louisiana Museum of Modern Art. Archaeological artefacts at Bihar Museum help visitors explore the region’s past, from early civilisations to later historical periods. Photograph: ( Instagram/@mrincoder & @aspectrum ) Russia’s State Hermitage Museum ranks fourth, while Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum takes fifth place. Turkey’s Şanlıurfa Archaeology Museum is sixth, followed by Poland’s Museum of the Second World War and the National WWII Museum in New Orleans, USA. The Met ranks tenth, while the Louvre is placed 31st. For its 2026 edition, Worth a Journey says it analysed more than one million venues to create 36 lists of the world’s best places across travel and hospitality categories. Its museum ranking draws attention to destinations that may not always receive the same global recognition as their more famous counterparts. A reason to discover Bihar differently A museum visit can change how we see a place. A sculpture becomes a clue to an older civilisation; a piece of folk art opens a window into everyday life; and an architectural space brings centuries of history into the present. The museum’s spacious galleries and open courtyards make exploring Bihar’s history an experience beyond the exhibits themselves. Photograph: (Instagram/ @just.adulting ) At Bihar Museum, these stories come together in a setting that is distinctly contemporary yet deeply rooted in the region it represents. Its place among the world’s top 10 offers travellers another reason to put Patna on their itinerary. More importantly, it invites them to look beyond familiar tourist destinations and discover the many layers of India’s cultural heritage, one gallery at a time. ‘We Feared the Drive, She Loved It’: Delhi Mom Shares ‘Surprises’ From 800-Km Road Trip With Toddler
stories.summary: Somewhere between Delhi and Kashmir, a two-and-a-half-year-old found herself waiting for tunnels to appear, pointing out sheep and monkeys by the road , and watching mountains, rivers and rain unfold outside the car window. For her parents, it was an 800-km road trip. For her, it was a moving picture book she couldn't stop asking questions about. For Akanksha Khullar, the journey had begun with a very different feeling: apprehension. Could they really drive all the way to Kashmir with a toddler? Would she manage the long hours in the car? Would the carefully planned itinerary hold up once they were on the road? Reflecting on that initial fear, Akanksha says, “It’s important to show your child the possibilities that exist. And your fear is the key one.” As it turned out, the daughter, whom they had worried about keeping entertained, was often the most curious traveller in the car. “She was so curious about what she was seeing and experiencing,” Akanksha recalls. “There was so much greenery, so many animals just out there. She would ask, ‘Which animal is this?’ and then create a story around it.” From tunnels and winding mountain roads to rivers and rain, the changing scenery kept Akanksha’s two-and-a-half-year-old daughter curious throughout the drive. For Akanksha, a writer and storyteller who works as an advisor at the Royal Norwegian Embassy, those little questions became some of the most memorable parts of the trip. They were also what she had hoped for when the family decided to travel by road: a chance for her daughter to experience travel differently. Why they chose an 800-km drive over another flight  Travel has always been a part of Akanksha and her husband's life. Their daughter had already travelled internationally, including her second international trip when she was six months old. But as Akanksha's daughter grew older and started going to day school, the family found themselves thinking differently about summer holidays. “We realised that we've only given her that international exposure,” she says. “We have family throughout North India, but somehow our international trips had been more than our domestic ones.” The summer holidays presented another challenge. Much of North India was hot, while popular hill stations were crowded. The couple began researching possible destinations. They considered several destinations, including Shimla and other hill stations, but Akanksha and her husband wanted to explore somewhere different this time. Rather than rushing through multiple destinations, the family kept their Kashmir itinerary limited to Srinagar and Pahalgam, allowing them to travel at a relaxed pace. “We were very sure that this time we didn't want to do a flight thing with her because we've been doing that a lot,” she says. “For us, it was almost like making her relearn what travel is.” That meant getting into the car and driving, maybe all the way to Kashmir. Planning the road around a toddler An 800-km road trip is a considerable journey for anyone. With a toddler, Akanksha knew they couldn't simply plan the route around distance and sightseeing. Her daughter's meals, breaks and comfort had to be part of the itinerary too. “There was a lot of strategic planning that went into the whole process,” she says. They carried snacks, planned activities and thought carefully about when to start driving and where to stop. The journey was broken up according to their daughter's schedule rather than simply trying to cover as many kilometres as possible. The family was also travelling in an electric vehicle, which added another layer to the planning. Charging stops had to be factored into the journey, but some of them became enjoyable breaks for their daughter too. Charging stops during the family’s electric vehicle journey became opportunities for their daughter to take a break and observe the world around her. Akanksha's husband enjoys studying cars and planning routes, so they mapped their charging stops carefully. As it turned out, several of the places where they stopped for charging also worked well for their daughter. “Having an EV and a super high-tech car is a blessing,” Akanksha says. “We knew the journey was going to be very smooth.” At one stop in Karnal, her daughter watched ducks. Along the route to Srinagar, the mountains, rivers and tunnels gave her plenty more to look at. Even the charging stations became memorable. On the trip, Akanksha says, her husband ended up helping other EV owners charge their cars. The biggest surprise? Their daughter loved the long drive  Before leaving, one of Akanksha's biggest concerns was the car journey itself. “How is a two-and-a-half-year-old going to manage such a long journey?” was the worry. But once they were on the road, something surprising happened. “The car journey was the smoothest,” she says. Her daughter was fascinated by the changing scenery. She watched the tunnels, noticed when the road went “up” and “down”, looked at the rain, and kept asking questions. The journey also gave Akanksha and her husband something they don't always get on an ordinary day: uninterrupted one-on-one time with their daughter. Both parents drove, so they could split the driving. When one parent was behind the wheel, the other could sit with their daughter. Playing football on a lawn and spending uninterrupted time together became some of the simple pleasures of the trip. “She would just come up with something,” Akanksha recalls. “ These tiny moments that you would not get on a regular day. It was so precious.” There were also moments when their daughter wanted some time with one parent. Sometimes it was “Dad, let's do this” and sometimes she would just lie down and enjoy the ride. For Akanksha, these small, unscripted moments became some of the most memorable parts of the trip. When food and motion sickness tested their plans The car journey had gone better than expected, but the trip still had its messy moments. Food, in particular, turned out to be more challenging than Akanksha had anticipated, especially in Kashmir. And on the return journey, her daughter experienced motion sickness. Thankfully, Akanksha had packed extra clothes, newspapers and bags after someone had warned her it might happen. It did. More than once. “It happened once; I changed her clothes, and then it happened again and again,” she laughs, remembering the episode. By the fourth time, the parents had adapted. “We were like, okay, now we're going to sit with a flip-flop in our hand,” she recalls. For Akanksha, that was another lesson in travelling with a young child: preparation matters, but so does the ability to adapt when the plan falls apart. “You learn and you adapt,” she says. “It's all patience. A lot of patience. You have to centre yourself again and again.” Keeping Kashmir slow Once they reached Kashmir, the family chose to keep their holiday relaxed. They kept their itinerary limited to Srinagar and Pahalgam. After all the planning and driving, Akanksha and her husband wanted a slower trip for themselves too. This gave them time to enjoy Kashmir at their own pace, with room for the little things: playing football together on a lawn, spending time as a family, and simply being present. ‘You don’t realise how solid a team you are as parents’ Looking back, Akanksha remembers the joy alongside the challenges. She also recognises that an 800-km road trip with a toddler may not suit every family. She believes parents can sometimes underestimate what their children are capable of experiencing. “I don't know if I would advise it to anybody,” she says, acknowledging that their experience was possible in part because she had a supportive partner who was completely on board. “But the point is that it's important to show your child the possibility that exists.” Akanksha’s family road trip to Kashmir taught them to embrace the unexpected and enjoy the journey together. For Akanksha, the biggest hurdle was her own fear. “I was very jittery. I couldn't believe that we were doing this,” she says. And yet they did. The journey also gave the couple a new understanding of themselves as parents . In the busyness of everyday life, they hadn't necessarily stopped to notice how well they functioned as a team. “This whole thing gave us a lot of confidence in our journey of being parents also,” she says. “You don't realise how solid a team you are as parents.” Her daughter may not remember every kilometre of that 800-km journey. She may not remember the charging stations or the exact roads they took. But she saw mountains, rivers, animals and tunnels. She asked questions. She watched the world change outside the window. She spent time with both her parents. For Akanksha, those are memories she will carry with her for years. “Twenty years down the line, when I look back, I would just be like, damn. This was one good trip.” All images courtesy Akanksha Khullar

stories.title: Can Chennai's Water Solution Save Hyderabad From Water Crisis?
stories.summary: #thebetterindia Hyderabad is facing a serious water crisis. One of its main reservoirs has dropped to just 13%, and 6,000 water tankers are being booked every day. But what if the solution lies in a simple idea that helped Chennai fight its own water crisis? In 1995, Professor Sekhar Raghavan noticed something alarming. His tap water had turned salty because falling groundwater levels allowed seawater to seep in. Chennai received plenty of rainfall, but much of that water was going to waste. Instead of waiting for someone else to act, he began promoting rainwater harvesting. His idea was simple: collect rainwater from rooftops, driveways and other surfaces, filter it, and allow it to recharge underground aquifers. He cycled door to door, convincing residents to adopt the system. Many dismissed his efforts. But he persisted. In 2003, Tamil Nadu made rainwater harvesting mandatory in buildings. Groundwater levels reportedly rose by nearly 20 feet, helping Chennai improve its water security. For around 15 years, the city benefited from this approach. But there was a problem. Poor maintenance, clogged filters and neglected recharge pits weakened many systems. When Chennai faced another severe drought in 2019, the city once again came dangerously close to running out of drinking water. Today, Chennai is exploring solutions such as sponge parks and underground rainwater capture systems to strengthen its water resilience. The lesson? Rainwater harvesting isn't just about installing systems. It's about maintaining them, protecting groundwater and making every drop count. With Hyderabad facing mounting water stress, could Chennai's experience offer a way forward? Should Hyderabad make rainwater harvesting a bigger priority? stories.title: ‘Who Checks If Govt Officials Are Declaring Their Wealth Correctly?’: RTI Activist Explains 4 Key Steps
stories.summary: Imagine a dozen people asked to write down what flats in the same apartment block are worth, and each gives a different figure. That is roughly what an IndiaSpend analysis found among Indian Foreign Service officers. At least a dozen of them had declared sharply different values for flats in the same apartment block in Delhi's Mayur Vihar. Each had filed a return as the rules demanded, yet the differences raised an important question: who was checking whether the values were accurate? "That gap between filing a declaration and proving it honest sits at the centre of how India tries to police the wealth of its public servants. Every public servant covered by the Lokpal law must declare assets and liabilities, but the form is only the first link in a longer chain of checks," explains L. Chakrapani, a Chennai-based RTI activist and former senior advocate at the Madras High Court . Someone has to read these returns, compare them with lawful income and act when the numbers don't add up. Here is how that chain is supposed to work, what the rules actually require today, and where it gets weak. What officials have to declare Under Section 44 of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, every public servant covered by the Act is required to declare their assets and liabilities in the form and manner prescribed by the government. The original law required annual returns by 31 July and directed ministries or departments to publish the statements on their websites by 31 August, as set out in a Department of Personnel and Training order. However, the 2016 amendment replaced Section 44 and removed these specific requirements from the Act.   Under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, asset declarations were intended to help bring public servants’ wealth under scrutiny.   In December 2016, the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) said that returns under the amended Lokpal provision did not need to be filed until fresh rules were notified. In September 2022, it confirmed that those rules had still not been issued. Under the original Lokpal framework, the declaration covered the whole household. It included the assets and liabilities of the officer's spouse and dependent children. Officers of the IAS, IPS and Indian Forest Service already had a similar duty under the All India Services conduct rules, which ask for a return on first appointment. An India Today investigation reported that the return must list immovable property, shares, debentures, postal time deposits, cash including bank deposits, other movable property, and debts and liabilities. It also noted that the rules cover property held in an officer's own name, a family member's name, or anyone else's name. These service-specific requirements continue to matter even where the separate Lokpal declaration framework has been delayed. For example, IPS officers must file annual immovable property returns by 31 January under the All India Services conduct rules.   Filing property returns creates a record against which an officer’s wealth can be compared over time. Photograph: ( The Hindu )   That last part is telling. The rulebook also accounts for the possibility of officers holding wealth through other people, which is why the checks after the form matter as much as the form itself. Check one: Did the form even arrive? This is the simplest check, because authorities can identify who has failed to submit a required return. The Central Vigilance Commission has told central government officials that not filing property returns gives "good and sufficient reasons for instituting disciplinary action". It expressed deep concern over prolonged delays and in 2020 set 30 November as the deadline for 100% compliance. Even ministers have been late. Hindustan Times previously reported that 14 cabinet ministers and 21 junior ministers in a 77-strong council had not made their assets public, six weeks after the August deadline for declaring them to the Prime Minister.  "There should be a mechanism to scrutinise the declarations. Otherwise there is a weakness that every later check tries to fix, since a filed form proves only that someone filled it in," Chakrapani says. The distinction matters. Treating a missing return as misconduct means officials can't wait for an investigation to begin before answering for the omission. Filing also creates a record to measure against later. "Filing gives authorities a baseline, because every later year can be compared with the one before it. Without that baseline, no one can say that wealth has grown faster than income, which is the question that the criminal law eventually asks," he explains. Check two: Are the numbers true? A form can be complete and still be wrong, which is why the differences reported in the Mayur Vihar declarations deserve scrutiny. IndiaSpend asked whether the real worry was that officers misstated values or "just don't care". For ordinary citizens, even seeing these forms has been a struggle. India Today reported that it took "two years of argument and persuasion" with the Department of Personnel and Training and the Central Information Commission, through the RTI route, to obtain just the immovable assets of around 120 secretary-rank officers. That was before the Lokpal Act originally introduced a requirement for ministries to publish annual statements. Although the 2016 amendment removed that requirement from Section 44, property returns filed under certain service rules are still published by the relevant departments.   The Prevention of Corruption Act provides for action against public servants who cannot satisfactorily account for disproportionate assets. Photograph: ( Deccan Herald )   It shows why public access has always been part of the story. "Realistic verification rests on comparing declarations with independent records, mainly income-tax data, since the CBDT already cross-checks elected representatives' affidavits and reports any discrepancies. This rests on the CBDT and Election Commission framework, covered by the Lawyer E-News report, and on the CBDT's 2017 affidavit to the Supreme Court," Chakrapani tells The Better India. For elected representatives, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) and the Election Commission of India (ECI) have a joint framework for verifying election affidavits. It allows asset disclosures to be checked against tax information and discrepancies to be investigated, according to a Supreme Court order reported by Lawyer E-News. In a September 2017 affidavit to the Supreme Court, the CBDT said it had begun investigating seven Lok Sabha members and 98 assembly members after finding discrepancies in their declarations. The Court had pulled up the government over members whose wealth showed "a massive jump". The department said details would go to the court in a sealed cover, since income-tax investigations are exempt under the transparency law. These checks concern election affidavits filed by candidates. They are distinct from the property returns filed by civil servants, although both raise the same question about independent verification. Check three: What if an official's wealth grows faster than their income? Once a discrepancy surfaces, the Prevention of Corruption Act gives investigators a legal test. The offence has a long history. Section 5(1)(e) of the 1947 Act criminalised property disproportionate to known income, and Section 13(1)(e) of the 1988 Act carried the idea forward before the 2018 amendment recodified it. Section 13(1)(b), as substituted by an amendment that took effect on 26 July 2018, makes it an offence to enrich oneself illicitly during the period of office. The law presumes illicit enrichment when a public servant, or anyone on their behalf, holds money or property disproportionate to known sources of income that they cannot satisfactorily account for. "The Act defines known sources of income as income from lawful sources, which means gifts, loans and savings count only if they can be shown to be lawful. A conviction carries imprisonment of not less than one year and up to seven years, and a fine," Chakrapani says.   Tax records and independent financial checks can help investigators identify discrepancies between declared assets and lawful income. Photograph: ( The Hans )   The current Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, however, provides for imprisonment of four to ten years, along with a fine. The punishment was increased from the earlier one-to-seven-year range through an amendment effective from 16 January 2014. The Lokpal can act too. According to Nyaaya, its inquiry wing conducts an initial inquiry into corruption charges against a public servant, and the Lokpal can then file a case before a Special Court. PRS Legislative Research notes that the Lokpal holds power of superintendence over the CBI for cases it refers. This is where the declaration becomes evidence. It records what an officer owned on a given date and who else held property for the family. "A case can then succeed when investigators rebuild lawful income, loans, gifts and savings across the check period, and fail when that accounting has gaps," he says, drawing on his own litigation experience. Check four: Will the evidence hold up in court? Courts examine disproportionate assets cases in two stages. According to a legal analysis published by Casemine, the prosecution must first establish the disproportion. Only then does the burden shift to the accused to account satisfactorily for the assets. A High Court ruling reported by Taxguru shows how this plays out. The court set aside the conviction of two public servants in Chennai because the prosecution had not properly accounted for their legitimate income, loans, gifts and savings. It held that the defence had shown the properties came from lawful sources.   Photograph: (AI-Generated)   A strong case, then, needs more than a list of properties. Investigators must rebuild a full income and expenditure picture across the entire check period. According to Chakrapani, this is also why accurate declarations matter, since a truthful record of loans and gifts made years earlier can support or undercut a later explanation. Who is monitoring the growing wealth? The system has one gap that courts have already noticed. On 16 February 2018, a Supreme Court bench of Justices J Chelameswar and S Abdul Nazeer directed the creation of a permanent mechanism to monitor the assets of legislators that grow disproportionately to their known income. The bench said such assets "should alarm citizens and voters of any democratic society", according to LiveLaw. The Wire reports that the same bench refused a one-time investigation of named legislators, calling that "selective witch-hunting". It asked for monitoring of legislators whose assets rose by more than 100% by the next election, with findings reaching the appropriate legislature. Lok Prahari later filed a contempt petition, arguing that the government had not complied with several directions. The Wire reported on 24 April 2026 that the Supreme Court had disposed of the petition on 16 April 2026, after finding no wilful disobedience. The permanent mechanism had still not been created eight years after the original judgment. During the proceedings, the Union government pointed to an existing framework between the ECI and the CBDT for verifying asset disclosures. The Court accepted that contempt had not been established, bringing the proceedings to a close. In practice, that leaves verification to existing agencies, which act on complaints, tax discrepancies and criminal investigations. What this means for you The four checks show the different stages at which an asset declaration can be examined, although they do not necessarily follow one fixed sequence in every case. The first confirms that officials file, the second tests whether the numbers hold up, the third compares them with lawful income, and the fourth tests the evidence before a judge. A weak link anywhere can leave a questionable declaration unexamined. For citizens, the practical test is whether these stages are visible. Published returns, publicly reported verification findings and open court proceedings are among the ways outsiders can observe how the system is working. The Lokpal Act originally set the 31 July deadline, while other service rules continue to require property declarations. The Prevention of Corruption Act provides criminal penalties for illicit enrichment. The space between them depends on who is willing to read the forms. A declaration builds accountability only when someone checks it against income and acts on what they find. Eight years after the Supreme Court called for permanent monitoring of legislators' wealth, that mechanism remains absent. The question now is whether the existing checks can provide the scrutiny that the Court had sought. stories.title: He’s 100 & Still Practising Law: The Guinness World Record Holder With a Rare High Court Honour
stories.summary: A 100th birthday usually calls for cake and candles, yet P Balasubramanian Menon, a lawyer from northern Kerala’s Palakkad district, received something rarer and rather more formal. On 9 October 2026, six days before he turned 100 on 15 October, the Kerala High Court approved his designation as a Senior Advocate, timing the decision to coincide with the milestone itself.  Chief Justice Soumen Sen began the initiative, and Bar and Bench reported that this might be the first time the court has conferred the rank on a lawyer who practises before the mofussil courts, which sit below the High Court.  Bar and Bench calls Menon a trial lawyer, a practitioner who argues disputes before the courts that hear them first. Under Section 16 of the Advocates Act, 1961, India has two classes of advocates, senior advocates and other advocates. A High Court may formally designate an advocate as senior, with the advocate’s consent, if it considers that ability, standing at the Bar or special knowledge or experience in law makes him deserving of the distinction.  By approving the designation, the Kerala High Court formed that opinion about Menon after more than 76 years in practice. From Madras to Palakkad To understand the honour, it helps to look at where his career began and how it changed direction. Menon comes from a traditional family in Palakkad and studied law at Madras Law College before he began his career in 1950 at the Madras High Court , where he trained under Advocate General Kuttikrishnan Menon. After two years, he returned to Palakkad and worked under the criminal lawyer KS Ramakrishna Iyer.  Bar and Bench’s 2023 interview records that, like many lawyers of his generation, he had not made law his first choice.   The Kerala High Court designated Menon a Senior Advocate on 9 October 2026, days before his 100th birthday. Photograph: ( Bar and Bench )   His early cases were criminal, but an encounter with a judge during a case in Kochi encouraged him to specialise in civil law, which has been his focus since 1952 and remains his main area of practice. LiveLaw reported in 2023 that he continued to practise on the civil side in his hometown. How 73 years of practising law earned him a world record  His office, as Bar and Bench described it in 2023, has an old-world charm and countless mementoes, the latest being the Guinness World Record, while a second certificate in a glass frame marks the Indian Book of Records recognition that came a few months earlier. Guinness World Records verified his career in Kerala at 73 years and 60 days on 11 September 2023, making him the holder of the title for the longest career as a lawyer (male). Asked by Bar and Bench whether he had ever imagined such recognition, he said not even in his dreams. Menon surpassed the record set by Louis Triay, a Gibraltar lawyer whose record stood at 70 years and 311 days, according to LiveLaw. Triay died in February 2023 at the age of 94, months before Guinness World Records verified Menon’s career.   From beginning his career at the Madras High Court in 1950 to practising in Palakkad, Menon has spent decades arguing civil cases. Photograph: ( Facebook/Suma Kanakala )   PTI reported in November 2023 that, with the enthusiasm of a much younger lawyer, he went to his office and the courts every day without fail, met clients and kept his arguments and cross-examinations brief, even at 97. He describes his duty to clients in terms of trust, telling a television channel, “When a party approaches me with a case, he is coming by trusting me.” At 100, he still has no plans to retire  Three numbers recur in Menon’s story, and each measures something different: his age of 100, his more than 76 years of practice according to Bar and Bench, and the 73 years and 60 days that Guinness verified on 11 September, 2023. The gap between the two shows his career continued well after Guinness took its measurement. In the 2023 interview, when he was in his 98th year, Menon said, “I am running 98. I am not even thinking of retirement.” He added that he still works to earn his livelihood, and PTI noted that he smiles gently when anyone asks about retirement. The Senior Advocate rank now joins the Indian Book of Records certificate and the Guinness title among the formal recognitions of a career that began in 1950.  Menon has said that he hopes the record can inspire others, and his story offers them a gentle lesson: a lawyer who keeps his arguments brief, answers to his clients’ trust and smiles when asked about retirement has built the longest career Guinness has verified for a male lawyer, one patient year after another. stories.title: Why People Paint Themselves as Tigers & Dance Through the Streets of Kerala & Karnataka
stories.summary: Before the tigers take over the streets of Thrissur, they have to be painted. For hours, artists cover performers’ bodies in yellow, black and red stripes. Masks go on, drums begin to beat, and on the fourth day of Onam, the ‘tigers’ dance through the Kerala city, prowling and pouncing before cheering crowds. These tigers are people, of course. But the animal they imitate has held a special place in local celebrations for generations. The tradition is called Pulikali, meaning ‘play of the tigers’. And hundreds of kilometres away, along Karnataka’s coast, another tiger dance carries stories of fear, admiration and protection. Together, these traditions offer a fascinating glimpse into how communities have understood and lived alongside the wildlife around them. How did tigers become part of Onam? Thrissur’s Pulikali is believed to be around 200 years old. Its beginnings are often traced to Sakthan Thampuran, who ruled Cochin from 1790 to 1805. Historical accounts offer different explanations of how the dance developed, reflecting the many cultural influences that shaped Thrissur’s public celebrations. Today, on Naalaam Onam, trained troupes gather with their bodies painted as tigers and leopards. They dance to the beats of traditional drums such as the chenda, thakil and udukku , sometimes acting out hunters pursuing tigers. Preparing for the performance takes hours of painting and practice. For the crowds that gather in Thrissur, the result is a celebration that brings the tiger into the heart of the city, year after year.   Artists spend hours having their bodies painted in elaborate tiger or leopard patterns before dancing to percussion instruments such as the chenda, thakil and udukku. Photograph: (Manojk) Why do people in coastal Karnataka dance as tigers? Along Karnataka’s coast, particularly in the Tulunadu region, a similar tradition called Pilivesha, also known as Hulivesha, brings painted tigers into the streets during annual celebrations. Performers paint their bodies in striking tiger patterns and dance through public spaces, keeping alive a tradition that has been passed down through generations. But what makes the tiger such an important part of these celebrations? The answer lies partly in the stories people have told about the animal for generations. In local folklore, the tiger has long represented strength, courage and protection. It has also been an animal people feared, particularly in places where communities lived close to forests. This relationship caught the attention of researcher Rohan Sharma. In a 2024 report for the Wildlife Conservation Society–India, Sharma spoke to performers, organisers and experts to understand Pilivesha’s place in local life. His research explored how the tiger became a powerful cultural symbol and how stories about the animal have influenced the way communities understand wildlife. The dance offers a window into the beliefs, memories and traditions through which people have connected with wild animals for generations.   Pilivesha documents a cultural relationship through which the animal occupies a place in community life beyond its biological presence in the landscape. Photograph: (Karthy shty)   Can these dances change how we see wildlife? Admiring a tiger during a festival is different from encountering one near a village, where people may fear for their safety or livestock. There is no evidence that performing Pulikali or Pilivesha directly prevents conflict with wild animals. But these traditions remind us that people’s relationships with wildlife have histories of their own. Sharma’s research suggests that conservation efforts can benefit from understanding local beliefs and listening to communities, alongside protecting habitats and addressing real safety concerns. After all, people who have grown up hearing stories about tigers may understand the animal differently from someone who has encountered it only through books or documentaries. When the drums stop and the paint comes off, the festival ends. Yet the stories remain, passed from one generation to another. And perhaps that is where these tiger dances offer their most meaningful lesson. By understanding why communities have long feared, respected and celebrated the tiger, we can begin more thoughtful conversations about sharing our world with wildlife. stories.title: 25 Years After Its Deadliest Cyclone, How Odisha Built a System to Get Entire Communities Out of Harm’s Way
stories.summary: As the wind gathers speed along Odisha’s coast, preparedness begins long before the first tree falls or the first road floods. For a family living in a low-lying village, it could mean knowing which shelter to reach. For a pregnant woman, it could mean moving closer to a health centre before roads become impassable. Cyclone Arnab has caused extensive damage along the Andhra Pradesh coast, while parts of Odisha continue to experience intermittent rainfall and strong winds. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has warned that the next 24 hours will be crucial, with the storm expected to move across Odisha towards southern Chhattisgarh, bringing heavy to very heavy rainfall and strong winds. The immediate priority is to protect lives. But Odisha’s response also reflects a decade of learning to live with cyclones. What does that learning look like on the ground? When the warning turns into action The IMD has issued a red warning for six Odisha districts: Nabarangpur, Rayagada, Koraput, Malkangiri, Gajapati and Ganjam. Extremely heavy to very heavy rainfall, accompanied by strong winds, is forecast in these areas. The initial alert cited wind speeds of 50–70 kmph in the six districts, while broader forecasts for the affected areas have indicated the possibility of stronger winds.   For now, the immediate task is to keep people away from dangerous coastlines, move vulnerable residents to safety and ensure rescue teams can reach those who need help. Photograph: (Odisha TV)   Bargarh, Subarnapur, Boudh, Nuapada, Balangir, Kalahandi, Kandhamal, Puri, Khordha and Nayagarh are also expected to receive heavy to very heavy rainfall, with winds reaching 40–60 kmph. Here is what Odisha has done so far:  Rail services have been disrupted, with more than 60 services reportedly cancelled across the affected network and others modified. Distant Warning Signal Number Two has been hoisted at Paradip and Dhamra ports, while Puri and Gopalpur ports have Local Cautionary Signal Number Three. Fishermen have been advised not to venture into the sea as conditions turn rough to very rough, with high seas expected along the southern Odisha coast. Schools and other educational institutions in affected areas have been closed, beaches shut to visitors, and restrictions on coastal road movement planned as part of the precautionary measures. The rescue teams waiting before disaster strikes One important part of cyclone preparedness is ensuring that help does not have to travel from scratch after the storm hits. Odisha has reportedly deployed 313 response teams: 60 Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force (ODRAF) teams, nine National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) teams and 244 Fire and Emergency Services teams. Personnel from these agencies, alongside the police, have been positioned in vulnerable areas to respond to emergencies. For now, the immediate task is to keep people away from dangerous coastlines, move vulnerable residents to safety and ensure rescue teams can reach those who need help. But these preparations are part of a much longer journey, shaped by disasters that exposed the cost of inadequate warning systems and limited evacuation infrastructure. A decade of lessons, tested by every storm On 29 October 1999, a super cyclone struck Odisha’s coast near Paradip with wind speeds estimated at 260–270 kmph. A storm surge more than 20 feet high, torrential rain, and widespread flooding battered coastal districts, washing away homes and cutting off communities from the outside world. Nearly 10,000 people died. Warnings did not reliably reach everyone who needed them, evacuation was limited, and there were too few shelters along the coast. In December 1999, Odisha established the Odisha State Disaster Management Authority. The Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force followed in 2001, creating a specialised force for rescue and emergency response . Over the following years, disaster planning increasingly involved identifying vulnerable villages, mapping evacuation routes, building shelters and preparing communities before a storm arrived. The difference became visible in October 2013, when Cyclone Phailin approached the coast. The storm was powerful, with winds reaching around 200 kmph or more, but the response was markedly different from 1999. VIDEO | Cyclone Arnab: Visuals from Gopalpur Beach in Ganjam, Odisha (11:08 pm, Tuesday). (Full video available on PTI Videos - https://t.co/d8jp61yd2p) https://t.co/qWTTHHfRX1 — Press Trust of India (@PTI_News) October 27, 2026 Authorities evacuated more than one million people across Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, moving residents away from vulnerable coastal areas and into shelters and other safe buildings. In Odisha, the reported death toll was far lower than during the super cyclone, although fallen trees, damaged homes and disrupted infrastructure still left a substantial recovery effort. Six years later, Cyclone Fani offered another test. The IMD began tracking the developing storm days before it made landfall near Puri on 3 May 2019, giving authorities time to issue warnings and organise evacuations. More than 1.4 million people were evacuated in Odisha. Fani still caused widespread destruction, with powerful winds damaging homes, electricity infrastructure and trees, but the death toll was contained to dozens. What preparedness looks like for people on the ground The measure of preparedness must go beyond the number of people evacuated or rescue teams deployed. For a family living in a low-lying village, preparedness could mean knowing which shelter to reach. For a pregnant woman, it could mean moving closer to a health centre before roads become impassable. As Odisha braces for the storm, the immediate task is to ensure that warnings translate into action across vulnerable areas. Rescue teams must be able to reach those who need help, and residents must be able to move to safety before conditions deteriorate. A decade of cyclone learning is not a story of better forecasts or more teams on standby. It is measured in the time a family has to leave before floodwater rises, the distance a pregnant woman must travel to reach medical care, and whether a village can get help when roads are cut off. The storm may pass. For the people living in its path, the quality of preparedness can shape what happens for months afterwards. stories.title: ‘Workers Were Risking Their Lives’: The Nagpur Architect Fighting for Their Safety, Toilets & Rights
stories.summary: When architect Samruddhi S Chaphale took a group of construction workers to a park in Nagpur for yoga, their smiles stayed with her. “One day, I took some of the workers to a park in Nagpur and got them to do yoga,” she recalls. “I could see how relaxed they became. There was a small smile on their faces, and that stayed with me.” She had met workers who spent their days worrying about wages, their families and the dangers of their jobs. That visit made her consider how rarely anyone asked about their wellbeing. “I realised that many of them had never really stopped to celebrate their own lives. They were constantly thinking about work, earning their daily wages and getting through the day. Earlier, their attitude was often, ‘Just give us the kit and let us go. We don't need anything else.’ But I realised they needed much more than a safety kit. They needed someone to ask how they were doing.” For Chaphale, founder of the Nagpur-based Levellers Foundation, this was a turning point. She began looking beyond the buildings she was trained to design, towards the people building them. When danger feels like part of the job Her concern began on construction sites, where she saw people working on roofs and at heights without adequate protective equipment. At first, she believed explaining the risks would help. “I realised that something was seriously wrong and extremely risky,” Chaphale tells The Better India . “I would see workers doing roofing work without safety kits. Initially, I thought it was simply a matter of explaining to them why they needed the equipment. I would tell them to wear their safety gear, but many of them were not willing to. They would just say, ‘Give us the kit and we will leave.’” As she spoke to more workers, she understood that providing equipment was only one part of the problem.   Levellers Foundation has worked with organisations on awareness around welfare schemes, housing programmes and land rights. Photograph: (Levellers Foundation -Screengrab)   “They had become so accustomed to risk that they had stopped thinking about their own safety. It wasn't that they didn't understand that something could go wrong. It was almost as if they had accepted that this was how their lives were going to be.” Chaphale is an architect, educator and advocate for socially responsive design. Through Levellers Foundation's Project Salamati, she works with architects, doctors, activists and community organisations to address the lives and working conditions of construction and garden workers. A helmet helps protect a worker's head, but it cannot provide a toilet at the site. Gloves cannot ease years of back pain, and a safety briefing cannot resolve anxiety about wages or housing. Salamati's approach grew out of listening to these connected concerns. When pain threatens a day's earnings Construction workers lift, carry, bend and climb for hours. Over time, repetitive work and injuries can leave them with aching backs, damaged joints and fatigue. For someone who earns through physical labour, pain can mean missed work and less money at home. A 2016 study in the Indian Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine identified musculoskeletal disorders as a major occupational health concern and described them as the largest cause of work-related illness. There were burdens Chaphale could not see as easily. She knew of a construction worker whose wife had died. He still had to earn while dealing with loss and the responsibility of feeding his family. The site, and the need for an income, carried on. Mental health became an essential part of her work. A 2016 study of 404 male construction workers in Kolar, Karnataka found that 27.5% had probable psychological distress and 14.6% reported poor quality of life . The lowest scores concerned their surroundings, including living conditions, healthcare and recreation. In a 2023 study involving 75 migrant construction workers in India , researchers identified 64% as potentially needing psychosocial care. Among those surveyed, 83% reported feeling unhappy and nervous, 75% had sleep disturbances, 71% struggled to think clearly and 69% felt tired or had frequent headaches. Thirty-nine percent reported having thought about ending their lives.   A 2016 study in the Indian Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine identified musculoskeletal disorders as a major occupational health concern and described them as the largest cause of work-related illness. Photograph: (Levellers Foundation-Screengrab)   These were small, specific groups, so their findings cannot represent every construction worker in India. They do, however, point towards pressures that discussions about workplace safety can miss. Chaphale says Salamati's own screenings revealed distress too. “In one of our screenings, more than 80% of the workers screened positive for depression,” she says. “One male worker was severely depressed.” “They are dealing with physical pain, financial pressure, uncertainty, migration, difficult living conditions and the constant pressure to keep earning. We talk about whether they have helmets and gloves, but we also need to ask whether they are mentally okay.” The questions women were beginning to ask For women on construction sites, Chaphale encountered concerns around washrooms, working hours, menstrual health and clothing. “I would see women working on construction sites where there were no proper washrooms,” she says. “Some of them were working late into the night. They wouldn't necessarily complain about it because they had already accepted those conditions as normal.” “I realised that sometimes I had to speak to the contractors because the workers themselves would not. They had normalised these conditions so much that they didn't always feel they could question them.” Conversations about menstrual health required patience and trust. “There was almost no awareness around menstrual health among many of the women workers I interacted with,” Chaphale says. “It was not simply about giving them information. We had to sit with them, talk to them patiently and understand their circumstances.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by Levellers Foundation (@levellersfoundation) She also spoke to women who wore sarees while working. “I remember having conversations with women who were working in sarees and explaining that while a saree is what they are comfortable wearing, it may not always be practical or safe for certain kinds of physical work. I would tell them, ‘Please consider wearing something that gives you greater mobility and safety, because your clothes can also become a risk at a construction site.’” She knew these discussions had to begin with understanding the workers' choices and circumstances. “You cannot walk into a community and tell people that everything they have been doing is wrong. You first have to build trust and understand why they do things the way they do. Once that trust develops, they start asking questions themselves.” Soon, some women wanted her to reach others in their neighbourhoods. “They started telling me, ‘Please come to our jhopadpattis [informal settlements] and talk to the other women too.’ That was important for me because it meant that they were no longer just receiving information from us. They had started recognising these issues themselves and wanted other women to know about them.” A safe place to live, and someone to care for the children Many workers Chaphale met had migrated to Nagpur and other cities from states including Madhya Pradesh and Bihar. Uncertain employment often went hand in hand with insecure housing. “They are migrant workers, and many of them live with the constant uncertainty that they could be asked to leave their settlement at any time,” she says. “When you don't have secure housing, you are constantly fighting for your rozi-roti [livelihood]. You are thinking about where your family will sleep, and whether you will still have work tomorrow.” India has a system of welfare boards for building and other construction workers, with protections now covered by labour codes that took effect in November 2025. According to the Union Labour Ministry , around 5.7 crore workers were registered with state and Union Territory welfare boards as of 30 June 2024. The boards had collected approximately Rs 1.15 lakh crore in cess and spent more than Rs 66,000 crore on benefits. But reaching those benefits can be complicated. “It is not enough to tell someone that a government housing scheme exists. We have to help them understand whether they are eligible, what documents they need, how they can register and what the process actually looks like.” Levellers Foundation has worked with organisations such as YUVA to build awareness of welfare schemes, housing programmes and land rights, and to help workers register with Building and Other Construction Workers welfare boards. “For them, registration can become a gateway to a number of benefits,” Chaphale says. “But if they don't know that these schemes exist or don't know how to access them, then the scheme might as well not exist for them.” The foundation is also exploring childcare support. “We are now looking at a creche for the workers' babies because childcare is another issue that people don't think about. If both parents are working on construction sites, what happens to their small children? These are all connected problems.” ‘Their lives matter’ One conversation with a 70-year-old worker showed Chaphale how deeply some workers had learnt to live with danger. “I once spoke to a 70-year-old worker about wearing safety equipment,” she recalls. “I told him that he had to wear a safety kit because the work he was doing was dangerous.” “He told me that he knew a friend who had fallen from a high-rise building and suffered a devastating head injury. And then he simply said, ‘It is okay. These things can happen.’” “There is a kind of nonchalance that comes from living with risk for so long. They start believing that accidents are simply part of their lives. They don't always feel that their own lives are important enough to protect.” Salamati is trying to challenge that acceptance of danger, while recognising that workers need support well beyond a construction site .   “We want them to understand that their lives matter. Their health matters. Their safety matters”, says Chaphale. Photograph: (Levellers Foundation-Project Salamati)   “We want them to understand that their lives matter. Their health matters. Their safety matters. They deserve to go home safely to their families. They deserve healthcare, decent working conditions, housing and knowledge about their rights.” A completed building may reveal the ambitions of a growing city. Its design shows how people will live and move within it. Behind it are the temporary shelters, missing toilets, workers balancing childcare and wages, ageing bodies still doing demanding work, and families unsure how long they can stay where they live. For Chaphale, the people who build India's cities deserve the same attention as the spaces they create. Their safety, health and dignity matter long after the building is finished.

A Sal Leaf, Some Clay & a Water Conservation Lesson: How Odisha’s Children Are Learning From the Forest
stories.summary: A curled leaf, a handful of clay and a shallow depression in the earth have become the starting point for an unusual water conservation experiment in the forests of Keonjhar district. The idea is: can children learn to hold on to water by observing how nature does it? A lesson hidden in a leaf On a walk through the dry forest slopes around Haladipani, a village in Odisha’s Keonjhar district a local elder stopped beside a curled sal leaf. Inside its cupped surface, a thin film of dew had collected, holding on to moisture even as the surrounding ground dried in the heat. For the children accompanying him, it was a small observation with a larger question behind it. If a leaf could catch and retain a little water, could they recreate that ability on the ground, where water was harder to come by? The elder, known locally as the ‘jungle master’, encouraged them to try. Instead of using plastic sheets or manufactured containers, the children began experimenting with sal leaves and clay to make small pits that could collect and retain water. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Village Square (@villagesquareindia) The experiment was documented by Biswabijayini Mohanty in a report published by Village Square on 16 September 2026, titled A Lesson in Water Conservation from a Leaf . The report describes how an observation made during a forest walk developed into a practical exercise in water conservation, with the children learning through trial, error and close attention to their surroundings. How the children made the pits The children dug shallow depressions near the forest edge using simple tools, sticks and their hands. But they soon encountered a problem: the loose soil absorbed the water poured into the pits before it could remain there for long. The jungle master helped them rethink the design. First, they laid broad sal leaves across the bottom and sides of each depression, overlapping them like roof tiles . They then spread clay soil over the leaves, pressing and smoothing it until the hollow took the shape of a shallow bowl. The two materials served different purposes. The leaf layer helped support the clay as it dried, while the compacted clay formed a lining intended to slow the movement of water into the surrounding soil. The children repeated the process, allowing the clay to set before filling the pits. Within about two weeks, they had created a network of small water-holding depressions along the forest edges. According to Village Square, the pits were generally no deeper than a forearm and rarely wider than a large dining plate. There was no plastic lining , costly equipment or elaborate construction involved. The materials came from the landscape around them, and the method evolved through observation and experimentation. When the rains put the idea to the test The pits were intended to hold water during the dry months. But after several days of rain, runoff carried loose soil down the slopes, turning surrounding water sources muddy. The pits, however, appeared to retain relatively clearer water.   According to Village Square, the pits were generally no deeper than a forearm and rarely wider than a large dining plate. Photograph: (Gadadhar Dehury-Via Village Square)   The explanation lies partly in the way water behaves when it is allowed to settle. Rainwater flowing over exposed ground can carry suspended particles of soil and other sediment. When that water collects in a relatively still depression, heavier particles can gradually settle at the bottom, leaving the water above them less cloudy. The report also records visits by wildlife, including barking deer, rabbits, mongooses and squirrels, which were seen drinking from the pits.  There is an important distinction, however, between water that looks clear and water that is safe to drink. The report does not provide laboratory test results establishing the potability of water collected in these pits.  What science tells us about sal leaves and water The principle behind the experiment has parallels in traditional agricultural practices documented elsewhere in Odisha A study compiled by Dr Prasanta Kumar Mishra, a principal scientist at the Central Research Institute for Dryland Agriculture, describes how tribal farmers in Pakanagaon village in Kandhamal district use sal leaves as mulch in turmeric fields. The account, published by LEISA India, notes that farmers spread a layer approximately 20–25 cm thick over their fields before the monsoon. The leaf cover helps conserve soil moisture, reduce runoff and soil loss, suppress weeds and protect the soil from the direct impact of raindrops.  Mulching works by covering the soil surface, reducing its exposure to direct sunlight and wind and helping slow evaporation. It can also reduce the force with which raindrops strike the ground, limiting the displacement of soil particles. Depending on the soil and rainfall conditions, this cover can allow more water to remain available in the soil. The Haladipani experiment uses sal leaves differently: rather than spreading them over agricultural land, the children place them beneath a compacted clay lining in small depressions.  Both of these practices show how locally available sal can be used to manage moisture and soil. The children are not simply being told that water is scarce or that forests must be protected. They are being encouraged to observe a leaf, understand what it does, test an idea and learn from what happens next. It is a practical starting point for environmental learning.  Sources: ‘Farmers’ practices of improving soil health by mulching in semi-arid india’ : By Dr Prasanta Kumar Mishra ‘Ground Report-A lesson in water conservation from a leaf’ : By Biswabijayini Mohanty, Published on 16 September 2026

From a 1972 Sorting Problem to DIGIPIN: The Story Behind India’s 6-digit PIN Codes
stories.summary: A letter for scientists at India's Maitri research station in Antarctica carrie the same PIN code as Panaji , 403001, because polar mail travels through the National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research at Vasco in Goa.  The quirk shows how much work six numerals do for the 1.64 lakh post offices that India Post operates today, and the story of that code begins with a sorting problem more than 50 years old. A country of similar place names At Independence in 1947, India had 23,344 post offices, mostly in cities, but the network had to keep pace with a growing country. The Postal Index Number, introduced on 15 August, 1972, aimed to ease the sorting and delivery of mail in a land where different places often share the same or similar names and letters arrive in a wide variety of languages. The idea came from Shriram Bhikaji Velankar, an additional secretary in the Ministry of Communications and a senior member of the Posts and Telegraphs Board. Velankar also wrote Sanskrit poetry, received the President's Award for Sanskrit in 1996, chaired the Indipex stamp exhibition in New Delhi in 1973, and retired from government service on 31 December, 1973. What each of the six digits tells you The length follows from the hierarchy of the code, which gives one digit to the zone, one to the sub-region, one to the sorting district, and three to the delivery post office. The first digit names one of eight regional zones, running from 1 for Delhi, Haryana, Punjab and Himachal Pradesh to 8 for Bihar and Jharkhand, while 9 belongs to the Army Postal Service.   Photograph: ( Hindustan Times /AI-Generated collage)   The second digit narrows the zone to a sub-region, and the third, read together with the first two, marks a sorting district headquartered at the main post office of the largest city in the area. Goa's 403 carves out a small piece of the 40 to 44 band that otherwise belongs to Maharashtra.  The final three digits identify the delivery office, and a busy office that splits in two receives the next available code. Each PIN maps to exactly one delivery post office, which receives the mail for every sub-office and branch office in its jurisdiction. A single PIN code can therefore cover a cluster of villages, and two neighbouring delivery offices share only their first four digits. The same code at the edges of the map The structure holds even at altitude, where the post office in Hikkim, a Spiti Valley village , stands at 4,400 metres and closes for six months each winter when snow cuts off the settlement. Its code, 172114, places it in Himachal Pradesh through the prefix 17, and the office ranks among the highest in the world.   The floating post office on Dal Lake began as a postal boat in 1953. It belongs to the same national network as any city head post office. Photograph: ( Lifeandtrendz )   The system also reaches Dal Lake in Srinagar, where the floating post office , which began as a postal boat serving lake communities in 1953, belongs to the same national network as any city head post office. The ninth zone serves a different kind of address, because the Army Postal Service runs field post offices serving the Army, Navy and Air Force across the country. The 2017 Salute a Soldier campaign, organised by India Post and the Postcrossing Society of India in Bengaluru, directed postcards of thanks to around 1,000 Army units. Why six digits still matter The model has a precedent abroad, because the United States introduced its Zone Improvement Plan code on 1 July, 1963, when letters passed through about 17 sorting stops. India followed nine years later with a hierarchy of its own, and its relevance remains clear whenever someone orders food or a parcel online. India Post has since added DIGIPIN, a 10-character code developed with IIT Hyderabad and ISRO that identifies a 4 m by 4 m square, and it complements the six-digit code rather than replacing it. The PIN still tells a sorter which zone, district and office should handle a letter, while DIGIPIN tells a delivery person which doorstep to find. Anyone can check a code using the lookup on India Post's website, and no PIN begins with 0, because the nine zones run from 1 to 9. Taken together, the digits turn an address into a route. A PIN such as 403001 tells a sorter that the mail belongs to the western zone, Goa's sorting district and the Panaji head office, and it does so without a word of any local language. That efficiency, which began on 15 August, 1972, still reaches from the largest cities to the highest hamlets. Sources ' Government expands postal network with 10,170 post offices over last 11 years ': by All India Radio News, Published on 10 December, 2025 ‘ What is DIGIPIN, India’s new high-tech address system from Dept of Posts? ’: By The Week, Published on 31 May, 2025
