Fed Up With Internships Asking for Fees, 21-YO Punjab Student Builds a Portal to Track Student Training
stories.summary: This article has been published in partnership with Vibha. For a student pursuing a diploma, an internship can be the bridge between what they learn in a classroom and what they will eventually do at work. But finding the right opportunity is not always straightforward. Nikhil Kumar, a 21-year-old B.Tech CSE student from Punjab, had come across internships that required candidates to hold a bachelor’s degree or pay fees to gain experience. After completing his diploma in 2025, he chose to pursue a bachelor’s degree. The experience made him think about the barriers other diploma students might face.  At Government Polytechnic College, Talwara, Nikhil was already putting his coding skills to use. Alongside his faculty mentor, Sukeeratpal Singh, he was developing a college management system to simplify administrative work. When Vibha’s Programme Management Unit (PMU) learnt about the project, it saw an opportunity to build on it. The team was working on a semester-long internship programme in which students would spend their final semester working in industry rather than attending regular theory classes. Together, they adapted the system to help colleges monitor students’ progress throughout this practical training. Sukeeratpal Singh and the Vibha PMU team helped Nikhil develop Place Intern to track students’ internship progress. Photograph: (AI generated using reference)   The project became Place Intern, a portal that brings student internship records, faculty visits and progress reports together. “I was also curious whether whatever I was building would be used in the real world,” Nikhil says. The project gave him the chance to find out. With guidance from his faculty mentor, Sukeeratpal Singh, and support from Vibha’s (PMU), which works with Punjab’s technical education department, Nikhil helped develop his college’s internship management system into a tool that could be used by other institutions.  How a college project found a purpose beyond campus At Government Polytechnic College, Talwara, Singh had been encouraging students to explore technology beyond their regular coursework. In 2023, he started a student club where interested students could spend additional time learning, experimenting, and helping one another. Nikhil stood out for his willingness to take on work independently. “He was always the one who finished the work first,” Singh recalls. The two began working on a college management system that could make certain administrative processes easier to handle. They planned its features, decided how it would work and tested it over several weeks. The project caught the attention of Vibha’s PMU when team member Abhay Vashisht visited the college. The team was working on the policy and programme design for a semester-long internship initiative for students in technical education.  As they considered how the programme would work on the ground, they began identifying possible implementation challenges, including how colleges could monitor students throughout their internships. Nikhil’s understanding of the college environment, combined with the PMU’s inputs on the internship programme, helped shape the portal into a tool that could support its implementation. Nikhil built the parts that store and manage information, tested the portal, put it online and kept it running. Singh helped him understand the college workflows the system needed to support, while the PMU team shared the programme requirements, developed an initial outline for the portal and worked closely with him to refine its design through testing and feedback. Place Intern brings student progress reports, faculty visits and internship records onto one platform, reducing dependence on separate spreadsheets and paper-based submissions.   Building the portal also meant learning how to work with the people who would use it. Nikhil showed faculty members how to use it, wrote instructions and made changes based on their feedback. He had to think about how different people would use the system and what information they needed to access. Place Intern currently helps colleges track students undertaking internships during their final semester, when they work in industry in place of regular theory classes. It does not serve as a placement portal that matches students with employers or guarantees them internships. Its four types of users each see the information they need. Faculty members can record monthly visits to students at their internship workplaces, while students submit reports on their progress. The principal closely monitors the tasks faculty and students undertake, while the Directorate in Chandigarh uses dashboard access to track progress and review updates. “By bringing these records together, the portal reduces dependence on separate spreadsheets and paper-based submissions,” adds Nikhil. Building the portal taught Nikhil how to create something people could actually use, and how working closely with those using it could help make it better. ‘Students need to apply their classroom knowledge’ For students like Nikhil, finding an internship is one part of a larger challenge: turning a technical qualification into the skills and confidence needed to enter the workforce. Mridul Dhyani, who works with Vibha’s PMU in Punjab, says diploma programmes have faced challenges around industry acceptance, student retention and employability. “Students may understand technical concepts in the classroom, but they also need opportunities to apply that knowledge and become familiar with workplace expectations,” he shares. For students in rural areas, finding these opportunities can be especially difficult. Colleges may have fewer employers nearby, and students may not have family or professional networks that can connect them to industries. Sukeeratpal has seen these challenges through his work in teaching and placements. Earlier, students often had to approach companies and establish industry connections themselves. Colleges also lacked a consistent way to track internships and follow students’ progress. Faculty members can use Place Intern to record monthly visits to students at their internship workplaces and track their progress during practical training.   “Earlier it was in the minds of the children that a diploma is enough,” Sukeeratpal says. “Now our priority has become to make the students job-ready.” Addressing these gaps means helping students find openings while also introducing structured internships, strengthening industry engagement, updating curricula and developing the communication and practical skills they need at work. Place Intern helps colleges keep track of students during their internships. Finding an internship is the first step, but colleges also need to know how students are progressing, whether their training is going as planned and if they are gaining useful experience. The portal is part of a larger effort to help students build the skills they need for employment.  Taking a student-built portal beyond the classroom The wider effort is supported by Vibha, which works towards ensuring high-quality public education for every child. Its mission is to improve learning levels in government schools by identifying, supporting and scaling proven solutions. It works with governments, implementation partners, educators and communities to strengthen different parts of the education system, including early reading and maths, teacher training, classroom materials, technology, record-keeping and tracking progress. In Punjab, the work focuses on technical education. “The underlying approach is similar: understand where the system is falling short, work with government teams and institutions to address those gaps, and support solutions that can become part of regular practice,” adds Mridul. The Programme Management Unit (PMU) helps put this approach into practice. Working alongside government departments and educational institutions, it listens to people at colleges, identifies what needs attention, helps develop solutions and sees them put to use. For Place Intern, the PMU saw how the college’s existing technology project could help manage semester-long internships. The team worked with Nikhil and Singh to understand what colleges needed, adapt the portal accordingly, and test and improve it for everyday use.  Through its PMU, Vibha works with Punjab’s technical education department and polytechnic colleges to bridge the gap between education and employment.   The aim is to make sure the tool works for the people who will depend on it. Faculty members, college leaders and department officials need to understand how it fits into their responsibilities, while students need a clear process for submitting reports and being monitored during their internships. “We just don’t work towards plans,” Dhyani says. “Our work starts with a plan, but it doesn’t stop till we complete the loop.” That follow-through matters when a solution is expected to last beyond its development. Training, feedback and institutional ownership can determine whether a new system becomes part of everyday practice or remains a one-off project. How a 2-week maths course became part of a bigger effort Alongside efforts to help students find internships, the wider initiative has also focused on making classroom learning more relevant to their needs. Across 91 government polytechnic colleges in Punjab, the wider initiative has reached 5,921 students in FY 2026, with semester internships introduced in six courses. These numbers reflect the initiative’s combined work across several interventions, not Place Intern alone. Some of the changes began with a simple question: what were students struggling with in the classroom? When mathematics emerged as a challenge, the team introduced a two-week bridge course to help students strengthen their basics. According to Dhyani, the results showed up the following year, when the proportion of students passing the subject rose from 16% to 31%. A two-week mathematics bridge course helped address gaps in students' foundational learning, with the reported pass rate rising from 16% to 31%.   English classes saw a change, too. Instead of placing most of the emphasis on literature and grammar, the revised curriculum focused more on functional English and everyday conversations. The reported pass rate rose from 45% to 92%. Dhyani recalls that some teachers were initially hesitant about the shift, but later noticed that students were participating more actively in class. The programme also includes faculty training, entrepreneurship education and efforts to build stronger industry links. Each intervention addresses a different gap, but the approach remains the same: understand the problem, involve the people affected and find a solution that works within the existing system. Singh has also seen how easily industry relationships can fall apart when they depend on a single staff member who later moves on. By keeping in touch with employers and sharing responsibility across staff, colleges can make these partnerships last and give students more reliable workplace opportunities. The next step: bringing colleges and employers together Place Intern has begun supporting the tracking of semester internships at the college level. Profiles for the first batch of more than 1,500 students have been uploaded, with profiles for a further batch of over 1,700 also being prepared. These figures indicate students being recorded for tracking, not that all have secured internships through the portal. The longer-term ambition is to make it easier for colleges and employers to connect. A planned statewide platform is intended to help industries share their requirements and allow institutions to identify relevant opportunities for students across polytechnics, industrial training institutes and degree colleges. For Nikhil, developing Place Intern has offered a different kind of practical learning. He has had to understand how people use technology, respond to feedback and keep a system functioning beyond its initial development. Beyond internship tracking, the wider initiative is working to improve functional English, strengthen industry connections and help students develop practical skills for the workplace.   Singh sees the project as a reason to give students more room to experiment, with faculty members providing the guidance needed to turn an idea into something useful. The next test is whether these systems can become part of everyday institutional practice, making it easier to monitor internships and build stronger links between education and employment. Nikhil’s experience began with developing a college management system, but working with the PMU gave the project a wider purpose. For Nikhil, the experience has meant building his own skills while working on a tool that could make the path from education to employment easier for students who follow. stories.title: Why Amur Falcons Choose to Stop in Northeast India: The Answer Lies in the Termites Found in the Region
stories.summary: Apapang, Alang and Ahu may weigh just 150 grams each, but they have some serious frequent-flyer miles to clock. They are Amur Falcons. In November 2025, these three Amur falcons were fitted with satellite tags by scientists from the Wildlife Institute of India (WII) in Tamenglong district, Manipur, to track their epic journey from Northeast India to Africa. Every November, thousands of these tiny birds of prey take off from roosting sites in Manipur and Nagaland , cross the Indian mainland and head over the Arabian Sea. Their itinerary? Thousands of kilometres, days over open water and no airport lounges in sight. Since the Amurs have created a mini-sensation with their incredible journey, I did a short Q&A with Dr Suresh from @wii_india who leads this remarkable tracking project. Here are a few fascinating insights Q. Why do Amur Falcons migrate? A. Migration is a natural survival strategy. Many species, including the Amur Falcon, move seasonally to escape harsh weather, seek richer feeding grounds, or find suitable breeding habitats. Over evolutionary time, individuals that migrated had higher survival and reproductive success which is why migration persists in certain species even today. Q. Why is tracking their migration important? A. Tracking with lightweight electronic tags helps scientists understand the exact routes and flight paths these birds follow, the environmental factors influencing their journey, and the critical stopover sites they depend on. It also helps identify threats along the way from habitat loss to hunting and provides vital insights into how Climate Change is shifting migration patterns worldwide. Q. How do Amur Falcons survive such long flights without food or water? A. Before they begin their transcontinental journey, Amur Falcons stop over at select sites in Northeast India, especially Nagaland and Manipur. Their arrival coincides with the mass emergence of termites a rich, high-protein food source. Here, they undergo hyperphagia or intense pre-migratory fattening, building reserves that sustain them through their nonstop oceanic flights where no food or water is available. Q. Do they take breaks while crossing the sea? A. No. Amur Falcons are terrestrial birds and cannot land on water. Once they leave the Indian coast, they undertake an uninterrupted flight across the Arabian Sea, a remarkable non-stop journey covering nearly 3000 km. — Supriya Sahu IAS (@supriyasahuias) November 17, 2025 Their journey revealed how a bird barely heavier than a smartphone can cross thousands of kilometres of open sea. It also highlighted why Northeast India is an important stopover along their migratory route. A journey tracked across continents On 11 November 2025, WII scientists fitted Apapang, an adult male, Alang, a young female, and Ahu, an adult female, with lightweight satellite transmitters weighing approximately 3.5–4 grams. The birds took flight the following day. The tracking updates were shared by Supriya Sahu, Tamil Nadu's Additional Chief Secretary for Environment, Climate Change and Forests, on social media. Apapang covered approximately 6,100 kilometres in six days and eight hours. Alang travelled around 5,600 kilometres in six days and 14 hours, while Ahu covered approximately 5,100 kilometres in five days before reaching the Horn of Africa. Their routes differed, but all three completed remarkable journeys across the Indian mainland and the Arabian Sea. Subsequent tracking updates placed Apapang in Tanzania, Alang in Kenya and Ahu in northern Somalia. The birds' journeys provided researchers with valuable information about their movements , flight durations and stopover behaviour.  Why do they stop in Northeast India? The answer lies in an insect that emerges in enormous numbers after the monsoon: termites. Amur falcons breed in parts of eastern Russia, northeastern China and Mongolia before migrating south towards their wintering grounds in Africa. During their autumn journey , Northeast India provides an important opportunity to feed and build up the energy reserves needed for their demanding flight. A 2024 study published in the Journal of Raptor Research, titled Prey Species in the Diet of the Amur Falcon (Falco amurensis) During Autumn Passage Stopover in Northeast India , investigated what the birds eat at their stopover sites.   The birds' journeys provided researchers with valuable information about their movements, flight durations and stopover behaviour. Photograph: (Bhupender Yadav-Wildlife Institute of India)   Led by researchers including Suresh Kumar of WII, the team examined approximately 1,200 regurgitated pellets collected at Pangti, Yaongyimchen and Hakhizhe in Nagaland during October and November 2017 and 2018. These pellets contained indigestible remains of the birds' prey. By examining them, researchers found that two species of subterranean termites, Odontotermes feae and Odontotermes horni , formed a substantial part of their diet. The findings help explain why the birds congregate in the region. Termites provide protein and energy that the falcons convert into fat reserves before embarking on their long oceanic flight. Researchers estimated that a million falcons could consume two billion termites in just over a fortnight.  A stopover that matters beyond autumn The importance of Northeast India extends beyond the autumn migration. In a second study, published in the Journal of Threatened Taxa on 26 March 2024, researchers Tapak Tamir, Abprez Thungwon Kimsing and Daniel Mize documented repeated summer sightings of Amur falcons in D'Ering Memorial Wildlife Sanctuary in Arunachal Pradesh. Here is the New Year Amur Falcon Migration -Very long Q&A Part II Q1. What is the longest non-stop distance covered by these satellite-tagged Amur Falcons? A: Published tracking shows Amur Falcons can do multi-day, non-stop flights of approx. 5,600–6,000 km during the India→Africa leg, depending on the individual & year. Also, peer-reviewed/technical tracking confirms their open-sea crossings can be about 2,364–3,138 km (Somalia↔India), typically completed in roughly 44–80 hours. Q2. Do satellite tags interfere with their flight, health, or mating? A: Properly fitted tags are designed to minimise interference, but no tag is “zero-impact.”. Best practice is to keep transmitter mass very small relative to body weight and use well-tested harness designs; the recent India work has been described as using very lightweight transmitters (a few grams). However, ethical review, careful fitting, and post-deployment evaluation should be done & is being done Q3. Do jet streams or high-altitude winds help them on this journey? A: Yes winds are a major part of the “physics” that makes the journey possible. The best-documented help is from seasonal monsoon tailwinds and strong, persistent wind systems over the Arabian Sea/Indian Ocean that can provide sustained push. Q4. How many other falcons are “accompanying” these famous three? A: These famous three are just the tagged individuals we can follow in reality, Amur Falcons migrate and roost in huge aggregations, often tens of thousands to over 100,000 at key stopovers, and broader estimates discuss movements involving very large numbers of birds across the flyway. Q5. Why have these three gone to different destinations? A: It’s common for individuals of the same species to winter in different areas within southern/eastern Africa. Differences can be driven by wind and weather, refuelling success and timing at stopovers, individual strategy/experience (age, condition, learned routes) etc. Q6. When will they return and what route will they take? A: In broad terms, Amur Falcons winter in Africa and then move north in late winter/early spring, reaching breeding regions in northeast Asia around May–June. Routes can differ between autumn vs spring, and tracking shows spring and autumn ocean crossings can follow different lines. Q7. Does part of the falcon’s brain “sleep” during the long flight? A: We have strong evidence that some birds can sleep in flight (including unihemispheric sleep) famously shown in frigatebirds. For Amur Falcons specifically, it’s not proven. Q8. How do they decide their destination, and do they return to the same places each year? A: The best-supported explanation is a mix of: Innate navigation programmes (genetically guided ) Environmental cues (winds, weather, geography, magnetic and celestial cues), learning/experience (older birds often show more consistent routes). Satellite work indicates the species follows remarkably consistent large-scale timing and corridors, even though individuals may vary. Q9. What do they eat to fuel such massive journeys? A: During the crucial Northeast India stopover, studies show they are highly insectivorous, with termites often dominant, along with other insect groups exactly the kind of high-abundance prey that allows rapid fattening before an ocean crossing. This is why protecting stopover habitats (and the insect “boom” they depend on) is so important. Q10. Is Ahu expected to move further? Why she is stationery ? A. Periods of little movement usually indicate resting or feeding in suitable habitat. This is normal behaviour and not a cause for concern Q11. How long does the GPS tag stay on the bird? A. The tag is fixed as a backpack & expected to stay for long, however this may come off from prolonged wear and tear, the tags may also stop transmitting after prolonged battery use. As told to @supriyasahuias by @sureshwii @wii_india #AmurFalconMigration video - The stopover tagging site in Manipur — Supriya Sahu IAS (@supriyasahuias) January 4, 2026 The sanctuary, in East Siang district, covers approximately 190 square kilometres and consists largely of grasslands, alongside riverine and subtropical forests.  The researchers documented sightings, including one in May, that suggested the sanctuary could serve as a refuelling site during the birds' return towards their breeding grounds. From hunted birds to protected visitors The falcons' journey has also become a story of community-led conservation. In 2012, large-scale hunting of Amur falcons around Pangti village in Nagaland drew national and international attention. In response, the Wildlife Institute of India, forest departments and local communities worked to understand the birds' migration and protect their stopover sites. Tracking efforts began in 2013. Over time, communities in parts of Nagaland and Manipur became important partners in protecting the birds. The falcons, once hunted in large numbers, increasingly became a source of local pride. Their migration demonstrates how wildlife conservation depends on connected habitats and people working across regions. A bird may breed in Asia, refuel in Northeast India and spend the winter in Africa, but its survival depends on the safety of each place along the way. For the Amur falcon, the seasonal emergence of termites is more than a feeding opportunity. It is a chance to prepare for a flight across continents. Protecting the landscapes where that preparation happens is essential to ensuring the journey continues. stories.title: Why Delhi’s Air Can Be Most Polluted Before 9 AM & What That Means for Your Morning Walk
stories.summary: The cool, quiet hour after dawn feels like the best time to step outside in October, yet AIIMS says pollution stays highest in the early morning until about 8:30 or 9 am. Delhi's air shows how quickly things can turn. At 4 pm on Tuesday, 20 October, the Central Pollution Control Board put the Air Quality Index (AQI) at 179, which counts as moderate. By 7 am the next day, the Air Quality Early Warning System showed 219, which counts as poor, and it forecast 342 for 22 October. The invisible lid above the city The explanation lies in physics. Normally, temperature falls with height, so air near the ground mixes and carries pollutants upwards. University of Reading researchers Ankit Bhandekar and Laura Wilcox explain that a temperature inversion reverses this, placing warmer air above colder air like a lid on a pot.  Pollutants stay near the ground, and the mixing height, the level up to which they can disperse, shrinks from about one kilometre in summer to a few hundred metres in winter. The lid sits lowest after dark. Sarath Guttikunda, founder of UrbanEmissions.Info, told Frontline that in November and December the inversion height can fall below 50 metres at night and hover around 200 to 500 metres by day. As the sun climbs, the layer lifts and the smog thins, which is why the early hours feel the worst. A bowl that holds on to smoke Delhi's geography makes this even worse. The city sits in the Indo-Gangetic plains, with the Himalayas to the north and the smaller Aravalli range to the south, which help create a natural bowl.    Delhi’s location between the Himalayas and the Aravallis, coupled with slow winds and little rain, allows pollution to linger. Photograph: (AI-Generated collage)   The Himalayas block air from flowing northward, so pollution must travel across northern India before it finds an exit over the Bay of Bengal. The monsoon rains that cleanse the air from July to September have gone by October, and winds slow down. Small shifts in weather can therefore tip the balance fast. Bhandekar and Wilcox note that on 5 January, 2025, favourable winds allowed authorities to lift some restrictions, yet by 15 January calmer winds and falling temperatures forced the city's strictest curbs. Delhi had not gained more cars, factories or construction sites from one week to the next. The Centre for Science and Environment also found something similar in winter 2023, when slow winds appeared to drive the most smog episodes in six years even though stubble fires in Punjab and Haryana nearly matched 2022. Solutions that follow the weather If weather decides when pollution turns, the Reading researchers argue, policy should follow the forecast rather than chase the smog.  They suggest tightening construction restrictions when inversions are predicted, even on seemingly clear days, and designing measures for the whole Indo-Gangetic plains, since many of India's most polluted cities share the same conditions.    Calm winds and falling temperatures can intensify smog even without an increase in vehicles, factories or construction. Photograph: ( The Print )   Delhi's Graded Response Action Plan already lets authorities act in advance on forecasts, with curbs ranging from dust control to limits on construction and vehicle movement. The other lever sits upwind, because smoke from stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana , where farmers clear fields quickly for wheat sowing, adds to the load each October and November. Some farmers avoid it by sowing wheat directly with a Happy Seeder , spraying a waste decomposer solution on straw , or selling paddy straw for conversion into fuel pellets . What you can do this season First, treat the cool early hours as the risky ones, since AIIMS advises staying indoors at peak hours and choosing indoor exercise over outdoor runs or cycling. Second, check the AQI daily on the SAMEER app, which AIIMS recommends, and wear an N95 mask if you step out.  Third, take extra care of children, older people and anyone with heart or lung conditions, whom the AIIMS advisory flags as most at risk. Fourth, skip driving once a week to trim local emissions, as AIIMS suggests. The advice does not reach everyone equally. Business Standard reports that an air purifier costing ₹12,000 to ₹15,000 is out of reach for many informal workers, and that indoor air can still hold up to 70% of outdoor PM2.5 without sealed windows and purifiers. That is why forecast-led curbs and cleaner fields matter as much as personal habits. Delhi cannot change the bowl it sits in or the chill that settles each night, but it can change what it puts into the air beneath the lid. With poor air forecast for 21 to 23 October, the next crisp, quiet dawn is better read as a warning than a relief. Sources: 1. He Failed 88 Times to Make an Edible Spoon. Now, It’s Finding Its Way to Dining Tables
stories.summary: At a Ganpati gathering in Mumbai, lunch was over and everyone was waiting for dessert. The thalis had been cleared, conversations had moved on, and there was only one thing left to do: bring out the kheer. Except this time, there was something unusual in the cutlery. Niki Rai, who had organised the gathering, asked her guests to hold on to their spoons instead of throwing them away. A few eyebrows went up. She had already told everyone that these were edible, but people were still understandably unsure. Then came dessert. “Now this is your biscuit,” Rai told the children, handing them their dessert with the spoon. The reaction was almost immediate. The children started biting into the spoons, treating them less like cutlery and more like a crunchy snack. The adults were more hesitant, watching first to see if it really worked. Soon, however, others wanted a taste too. “It was quite a spectacle, but it was worth it,” Rai recalls. The spoons had been made by Mumbai-based startup Edybites, which is trying to tackle a very ordinary problem: what happens to a disposable spoon after the few minutes it spends helping us finish a meal? Its answer is simple enough to eat. Founded by Rupesh K Sanghvi in 2022, Edybites makes edible spoons using a millet and flour-based formulation. The idea is that the spoon can become part of the meal rather than another piece of waste to be thrown away. If it is not eaten, the product is designed to naturally decompose. After 88 failed attempts, Sanghvi refined the spoon’s shape, texture and sturdiness to make it practical for everyday use. But turning that simple idea into a spoon that could hold its own through a meal was another story. It had to be sturdy enough to carry food, pleasant enough to eat and practical enough to make at a price people would accept.  The idea began with a spoon and a piece of khakra For Sanghvi, the thought first came during the COVID-19 lockdown. With fewer services and errands available, everyday household work suddenly meant doing much more oneself. One day, after preparing a meal and looking at a sink full of utensils, he found himself eating with his fingers because there was no clean spoon left. That brought back a familiar Gujarati food memory: khakra. “If we can finish our last meal of dal khichdi with a combination of khakra,” he thought, could something similar be made in the form of a spoon? The thought stayed with him. It also connected with something Sanghvi had observed during his more than 17 years in the aviation and travel industry. Having worked in sales and business development with airlines including Malaysia Airlines, Flydubai, Malindo Air and Kuwait Airways, he had seen how much disposable material moved through a flight. Once a flight landed, used food packaging and cutlery had to be discarded. Some meal components could not be reused because of safety and airline policies, even when they had not been consumed.   The edible spoons are designed to hold food during a meal and can be eaten afterwards, reducing the need for disposable plastic cutlery.   For Sanghvi, that raised a broader question : could at least one small part of the meal be made differently? He initially imagined the spoon being used with yoghurt, pastries, desserts or dishes such as dal khichdi and sambar rice on flights. Aviation remains one of the sectors he is interested in, alongside hospitals, institutional catering and events. The larger idea, however, is not simply to tell people to use less plastic. It is to make the alternative convenient enough that people actually use it. Making a spoon that does not fall apart That turned out to be the difficult part. Sanghvi says he failed 88 times while developing the spoon. Each version had to be tested for its shape, size, weight, and sturdiness. It needed to be strong enough to hold food, but not so hard that eating it became uncomfortable. The formulation uses a combination of sorghum, corn flour, and wheat flour, along with other ingredients. Sanghvi says the precise recipe is proprietary, but the millet and flour-based formulation is central to giving the spoon its structure. Too much flour, and the spoon could become soggy quickly. Too much firmness, and it could become difficult to bite. The team also experimented with flavours. Chocolate emerged as one of the main variants, particularly because it pairs naturally with vanilla ice cream. Edybites offers different flavours, including chocolate, which pairs well with desserts such as vanilla ice cream. That makes dessert one of the easiest places to introduce the concept. A person may be more willing to eat a spoon after finishing a bowl of ice cream than rethink every piece of cutlery used during an entire meal. There is also a practical reason Edybites has focused on spoons rather than trying to replace every disposable food item at once. Sanghvi says other edible products, such as cups, can face challenges when they are expected to hold liquids for longer periods. With tea or coffee, for instance, the material can soften or affect the eating experience. The spoon offers a smaller, more manageable starting point. The product has a shelf life of about three months without refrigeration, with the team working towards extending it further. It is made under a contractual manufacturing arrangement, with attention to hygiene and the heating process required to form the spoon. The finished spoons are individually covered and packed in boxes designed to minimise breakage during transportation. The product also requires the relevant food safety certification, including an FSSAI licence. When the spoon reached a real dining table For Niki Rai, the real test came not in a product demonstration but at a family gathering. Rai, a learning and development professional and executive coach, had first heard about the product through a friend. She was curious but wanted to try it herself before recommending it to others. When she eventually used Edybites spoons at a Ganpati gathering, she served them alongside a regular thali and asked guests to try them with the sabzi. Later, she brought them out again with kheer. The children needed little convincing. “For kids, it was like a biscuit,” she says. For adults, the experience was more about getting used to the idea. Rai says the spoon felt similar to a regular spoon and was comfortable to use, although its smaller size meant it could not hold a large quantity of food. She found it particularly suited to desserts, while children could use it for foods such as porridge too. At a Ganpati gathering in Mumbai, Niki Rai introduced Edybites spoons to guests, with children happily biting into them like biscuits after dessert. What stood out most to her was not just that the spoon was edible, but that it did not feel like a compromise. For Rai, taste was important. She also liked that the ingredients included grains such as jowar and wheat, along with fenugreek, rather than making the spoon feel like an entirely separate object that happened to be sustainable. Once the children started eating theirs, curiosity took over. The parents who had initially been apprehensive began joining in. Soon, Rai says, people were asking for extra spoons. Since then, she has continued recommending the product at events and gatherings, including while travelling. Making the sustainable choice practical There is, however, a catch. An Edybites spoon currently costs around Rs 7-8, according to Sanghvi. That is considerably more than a conventional disposable spoon, making price one of the biggest hurdles to getting people to make the switch. After all, when a plastic spoon costs a fraction of that, convincing someone to pay more for something they will eat or discard after one meal is not easy. Sanghvi has seen this play out in the conversations around the product. “However rich you are, at one point you would think, just to have a spoon, why should I pay seven rupees?” he says. That is why Edybites has not tried to rush into the mass market. Since November last year, when the startup began seeing stronger market traction, it has sold or distributed more than 5,100 spoons. For now, Sanghvi is taking a gradual route, exploring events, institutional catering, hospitals and airlines, along with markets where customers may be more willing to pay for sustainable alternatives. Edybites spoons blend sorghum, corn and wheat flour to create a sturdy yet easy-to-bite alternative to plastic cutlery. There is another irony to solve, too. The spoon is edible, but it still needs to reach the customer intact. That means packaging it carefully against moisture and breakage. Sanghvi says the team is experimenting with paper-based packaging and ways to reduce plastic without compromising the product. For a startup trying to eliminate one disposable item, using plastic to protect that alternative is hardly an ideal solution. It is a problem the team is still working through. What happens when a spoon becomes part of the meal? Perhaps the most interesting thing about Edybites is that its sustainability pitch does not end with the word “biodegradable”. It asks people to rethink what they consider waste in the first place. A conventional spoon has a very short life. It may spend a few minutes carrying a bite of food before being separated from the meal and sent to a bin. Edybites is trying to stretch that experience a little further: what if the spoon itself became the final bite? At scale, that could add up. Based on an estimated 2.5-3 grams of plastic in a conventional disposable spoon, Edybites estimates that every one lakh edible spoons could potentially displace around 250-300 kg of single-use plastic. At 10 lakh spoons, that works out to roughly 2.5-3 tonnes of potential plastic displacement. These are estimates of what could be displaced if the edible spoons replace plastic ones at that scale, rather than plastic waste already avoided by the startup. For Sanghvi, however, the number is only one part of the larger picture. He is particularly interested in what happens when children encounter such alternatives early. His hope is that edible or biodegradable options could eventually find their way into school canteens, hospitals, senior-care facilities and other places where disposable cutlery is used every day. And perhaps that is where Rai's Ganpati gathering offers a glimpse of what adoption can look like. Edybites has sold or distributed over 5,100 spoons and estimates that replacing one lakh plastic spoons could potentially prevent 250–300 kg of single-use plastic waste. The children simply needed to know they could eat the spoon. Once they did, the idea stopped being a sustainability lesson and became something much more familiar: a biscuit-like treat at the end of a meal. Rai has continued recommending the spoons at gatherings since that first experience, and her reason is simple. “We’ve got to be a flag bearer in our own way, no matter how small that change is,” she says. For now, Edybites is still figuring out how to make that small change cheaper, easier to package, and practical at a much larger scale. But somewhere between a Mumbai kitchen, 88 failed attempts and a group of children happily chomping through their spoons after dessert, the idea has found its most convincing test yet. The spoon did not end up in the bin, it ended up being dessert. All images courtesy of Edybites team

stories.title: 'I Spent 4 Years Farming on Weekends. Here Are 7 Things to Know Before Starting Your Own Organic Farm'
stories.summary: For years, Deepak Sabharwal knew food largely from the other side of the table. He had spent nearly two decades in the corporate world, working with companies such as General Electric (GE), PepsiCo, and Tata. His days were about meetings, numbers, and growth. Farming was something he spent time doing on weekends, at his family’s farms in Pushkar, Rajasthan. Then one day, he noticed the pesticides being used on his own farm . Around the same time, his mother was diagnosed with cancer. The two things came together in his mind in a way he could not ignore. “I began wondering what we were really eating every day, and that was a simple but uncomfortable question to ask,” he tells The Better India . That question eventually took him from boardrooms to fields. His hands-on farming journey began in 2012, while he was still working at GE, and he spent almost four years travelling to Pushkar on weekends to learn farming and experiment on his family’s land. Today, he is based in Delhi NCR and is the co-founder and CEO of Earthy Tales Organics Private Limited . The company was formally started in December 2018 with a focus on natural farming, farmer livelihoods, and making produce grown without synthetic pesticides and fertilisers more accessible to urban families. Deepak wanted Earthy Tales to do more than sell vegetables. For the co-founder, it was about fixing a disconnect he had begun to see between the soil, the farmer, and the person eventually eating the food. Years of working closely with farmers taught him that organic farming involves much more than avoiding synthetic pesticides and fertilisers. Here are seven lessons he wishes anyone entering the space would understand. 1. Start with the soil It is tempting to begin a farming business by asking one question. What should I grow? Deepak believes there is another question that should come first. What is the condition of my soil?   Today, Deepak is based in Delhi NCR and is the co-founder and CEO of Earthy Tales Organics Private Limited. Before investing heavily, he advises testing the soil and water, understanding what was previously grown on the land, and finding out which chemicals may have been used there. Because for him, organic farming does not begin with a label. It begins underground. “Organic farming begins with soil, not with certification or branding,” he says. A healthy farm may require compost, organic matter, mulching, natural inputs, better water management and, where appropriate, livestock integration. The aim is to move away from synthetic pesticides and fertilisers while gradually rebuilding the health of the land. That is also why he advises beginners not to convert an entire farm at once. He suggests starting with a small patch, trying a crop and observing how it performs over one or two cycles before taking the bigger plunge. After all, the soil has its own pace. A business plan cannot always make it move faster. 2. Build the whole system One of his early assumptions was that organic farming was largely about avoiding synthetic pesticides and fertilisers. He soon realised how incomplete that understanding was. Seed selection, soil health, water, compost, livestock, pest management, crop planning, harvesting, grading, storage, and transport all become part of the equation. “Natural farming is not only about not using chemicals. It is a complete system,” he says. And the work does not end when the crop leaves the field. It has to be sorted, packed, and transported. Some produce will be damaged. Some will not look perfect. Some may not sell in time. All of that has a cost. For someone starting, this is an important reality to understand. You are not simply starting a farm. You are building a system around that farm. 3. Earn farmer trust Getting a farmer to change the way they have farmed for years is not as easy as giving them a training session. Deepak learnt this by working closely with farmers. A farmer cannot treat a crop as an experiment.  A crop failure can mean a family’s income is affected. So when someone asks a farmer to reduce their reliance on synthetic pesticides or change farming practices, the farmer needs more than promises. “Farmers do not trust speeches. They trust consistency,” he adds.   The aim is not only to stop using chemicals, but to gradually rebuild the health of the land. That consistency can mean repeated visits to the farm, helping identify pests, discussing  what to do when a crop begins to fail , providing training and, most importantly, helping create a market for what the farmer grows. At Earthy Tales, the approach has involved working closely with farmers and supporting them in moving towards natural farming methods that rely less on synthetic inputs. The lesson is particularly important for entrepreneurs who want to work with farmers. If you want farmers to take a risk with you, you have to be willing to share some of that risk. 4. Find buyers first This was another lesson that took the co-founder time to learn. In farming, it is easy to fall in love with the idea of growing something. But a good crop does not automatically become a good business. “Natural farming must be market-linked. Otherwise, the farmer carries all the risk,” he says. So before sowing, an entrepreneur needs to think about the customer. What does the customer buy regularly? What can the region grow reliably? What price is realistic? How far does the produce need to travel? Who will buy it? At Earthy Tales, he noticed that many customers first came looking for fresh fruits and vegetables. Once they developed confidence in the source, they began buying everyday staples such as atta, pulses, oils, spices, and ghee.   The company was formally started in December 2018 with a focus on natural farming, farmer livelihoods, and making chemical-free food more accessible to urban families. That taught him something important about building a food business. Trust usually comes before the larger basket. A farmer may produce something excellent. But if there is no reliable buyer at the other end, the farmer still carries the risk. The market, therefore, cannot be an afterthought. It has to be part of the crop plan from the beginning. 5. Plan for uncertainty This sounds obvious, but it is one of the hardest realities for a business-minded newcomer to accept. Nature does not work according to demand forecasts. A farmer can plan for a crop, only for rain, heat, pests, or disease to change the outcome. Even when the crop does well, demand may not arrive at the same pace. Deepak remembers believing in the early days that good produce would naturally find its way to customers. “I believed that if we had good produce, the rest would follow,” he says. “But food does not work like that.” A crop arrives when it is ready, not when the customer wants it. It also creates a risk of wastage. Produce can be rejected because it is bruised, oddly shaped, or simply because there is more of it than the market needs that week. For a new entrepreneur, planning for unpredictable harvests and demand is essential. Crop cycles, storage and transport need to be flexible enough to handle surplus produce or unexpected delays. The more fragile the system, the more one bad season can hurt. 6. Know your numbers There is a natural temptation to think that a business built around a good cause will eventually work itself out. The co-founder has learnt otherwise. Organic farming can involve higher planning requirements, uncertain yields, wastage, packaging costs, logistics and working capital. If these numbers are ignored, even a business with the right intentions can struggle. “You cannot build a farmer-first business if the business itself is not financially sustainable,” he says. That does not mean reducing farming to profit margins. It means understanding that farmers cannot be supported by a business that keeps losing money. For him, the lesson is to calculate what each sale really costs, from sourcing and packaging to transport and wastage, before deciding whether the business can grow. The goal is to find a balance where the customer gets trustworthy food, the farmer gets a fairer return, and the business remains strong enough to keep going. 7. Give it time Perhaps the biggest investment an aspiring organic farmer needs is not money. It is patience. Soil may take time to recover . Farmers may take time to trust a new method. Customers may take time to change their buying habits. And a young business may take years before its systems begin to settle. Before investing heavily, he advises testing the soil and water, understanding what was previously grown on the land. The co-founder knows this personally. His own journey began with weekend trips to Pushkar while he was still working full time. For almost four years, he travelled between his corporate job and the farm, slowly learning what it meant to grow food. A good farm needs more than good crops  “Patience is not optional in this business. It is part of the model,” he says. That patience is also needed when things go wrong. A farmer may have a poor harvest. A crop may not sell. A transition may take longer than expected. A customer may question the price. The temptation is to look for a shortcut. But Deepak’s experience has taught him that there are very few shortcuts when you are trying to change something as fundamental as how food is grown. Deepak’s journey from corporate offices to farming has given him a broader view of an organic farming business. Growing crops without synthetic pesticides and fertilisers is only part of the work. The rest is making sure farmers earn a fair return, produce reaches customers and the business can keep going. For him, Earthy Tales is an attempt to bring soil health, farmer livelihoods and consumer wellbeing together. And for anyone thinking of starting an organic farming business, the question goes beyond how much they can grow. It is whether they can build a system in which the soil, the farmer and the customer all have a reason to stay. All pictures courtesy Deepak Sabharwal.

stories.title: 100+ Fashion Students in Haryana Turn Fabric Waste Into Art Without Using a Single Needle or Thread
stories.summary: A scrap of patterned fabric becomes a flower petal. Another, tucked carefully into a narrow groove, forms the sleeve of a Geisha holding a lantern. Across the classroom, students lean over thermocol sheets, trimming fabric, testing colour combinations and adjusting tiny pieces until their designs begin to take shape. Students carefully tuck fabric pieces into grooves cut along their thermocol sketches, bringing designs featuring flowers, landscapes and animals to life without needles or thread. At Budha College in Karnal, Haryana, more than 100 first-year Fashion Design students spent seven hours turning discarded fabric into colourful artworks, using a Japanese art form called kinusaiga. There were no needles or threads involved. Instead, the students tucked fabric scraps into grooves cut along their sketches, creating original designs featuring flowers, landscapes, animals and abstract patterns. Guided by their teachers, Harshita Singh and Komal, the students used fabric collected on campus to explore how leftover materials could find a new purpose. Turning fabric scraps into artwork Before picking up their fabric scraps, the students began with colour theory. They explored which shades, textures and patterns worked well together before deciding what they wanted to create. Once they had settled on a design, they sketched it onto a thermocol sheet and carefully cut grooves along its outlines. Then came the task of bringing the sketches to life. From selecting colour combinations to working with intricate patterns, the seven-hour activity gave students hands-on experience with textures, design and fabric reuse. The students sorted through the discarded fabric, searching for pieces that suited their designs. Each piece had to be cut to size and pressed into the grooves, with care taken around every curve and corner.  A small adjustment could change how a pattern looked or how neatly a piece of fabric fitted into place. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Budha College • Learn By Doing (@budhacollege) For Reya, a first-year fashion design student from Tamil Nadu, the assignment was an opportunity to experiment with an unfamiliar art form. She chose to create a Geisha holding a lantern, using fabric collected on campus to complete the design. “By upcycling waste fabric sourced from campus into the thermocol board, I created a piece I was genuinely proud of,” she says. Jahnvi, another first-year student from Jaipur, enjoyed experimenting with different colours, textures, and patterns. The exercise, she says, helped her explore art from a different perspective. Learning by doing The activity brought several aspects of fashion design together in one exercise: colour theory, an understanding of textures, material selection, and the patience needed to work with intricate details. For Harshita Singh, a faculty member in fashion design, the aim was to help students put classroom concepts into practice while giving them room to experiment with their own ideas. “As a mentor, I appreciate their patience, dedication, and creativity, because art is not just about creating something beautiful; it is about patience, passion, and enjoying the process,” she says. The students’ artworks, made using leftover fabric, reached a wider audience through Instagram reels that crossed 3.5 million views. The exercise also reflects Budha College's emphasis on practical learning. The skill-based institution, affiliated with Kurukshetra University, encourages students to build their abilities through assignments and projects alongside classroom instruction. According to CEO Abhinav, the broader aim is to help students become aatmanirbhar , or self-reliant, by developing practical skills they can carry forward after graduation. From a classroom assignment to millions of views The finished artworks found an audience well beyond the classroom. Reels featuring the students' creations crossed 3.5 million views on Instagram, giving the first-year students an unexpected opportunity to share their work with a much larger audience. Reshmi, a student from Bangladesh, said the activity gave the class a chance to express its creativity while working with discarded materials. Laxmi from Odisha initially found the technique difficult but said it became easier and more enjoyable with practice. The seven-hour exercise gave first-year students a chance to put their design skills to the test, turning classroom concepts into beautiful artworks. The artworks were created as part of a classroom assignment. They are not for sale and are not linked to a commercial venture or social cause.  The focus was on learning a new technique, experimenting with materials, and understanding how fabric could be reused creatively. By the end of the seven-hour exercise, the students had turned leftover fabric into individual works of art, each shaped by their choices of colour, pattern, and design. And without using a single stitch, they had found another way to work with material that might otherwise have been thrown away. All images courtesy of Budha College

stories.title: As Cyclone Arnab Approaches, What India Can Learn From Odisha’s Disaster-Ready Model
stories.summary: "If 90 mm of rain occurs in two hours, any city in the world will flood," says Dr Subimal Ghosh, Institute Chair Professor in the Department of Civil Engineering and Convener of the Interdisciplinary Program in Climate Studies at IIT Bombay, explaining that no city in the world, irrespective of the public infrastructure in place, can prevent flooding at that intensity of rainfall. For instance, Mumbai receives extreme rainfall (300-500 mm) in just three to four days every monsoon.  Ghosh believes the real question is no longer whether the city can stop flooding, but how quickly it can warn people before the water rises. And for that, he points to a model built 1,800 kilometres away, on India's eastern coast. A cyclone that changed everything On 29 October 1999, a super cyclone tore through Odisha with winds crossing 250 kmph, killing close to 10,000 people. It remains one of India's deadliest natural disasters.  Two decades later, cyclones of comparable intensity strike the same coastline and claim a fraction of the lives once lost, largely because of a warning and evacuation system built brick by brick since that tragedy. IAS officer Pradeep Kumar Jena , who has managed disaster response in Odisha for over 20 years, has spoken about the state's "zero-human-casualty" mission, a goal set after 1999 and pursued relentlessly since.    When Cyclone Fani, Odisha evacuated over a million people.   When Cyclone Fani struck in 2019 with wind speeds exceeding 200 kmph, the state evacuated over a million people and limited the toll to a few dozen deaths.  During Cyclone Amphan in 2020, of comparable ferocity to the 1999 storm, Odisha recorded only a handful of fatalities in the state, even as overall regional casualties stayed under 100. What the system actually looks like The Odisha State Disaster Management Authority, set up in 2000 as India's first dedicated body of its kind, anchors a layered warning network.  IMD forecasts and satellite tracking feed into a chain of over 800 multipurpose cyclone shelters and watchtowers across 120-plus coastal locations, from where sirens and mass alerts reach nearly 1,200 villages down to the last mile.  District collectors carry satellite phones and HAM radios so communication survives even when towers fall. A trained cadre of over 100,000 volunteers, alongside gram panchayats and women's self-help groups, runs evacuations and manages relief camps, while twice-yearly mock drills keep the machinery ready before cyclone season begins.  Dr Mrutyunjay Mohapatra, Director General of the IMD and an Odisha native, has led much of the country's cyclone forecasting work behind this system, calling accurate, lead-time forecasting the single biggest lifesaver. Why forecasting made the difference Structural fixes for urban flooding require geotechnical, structural, and water engineers working together over years, and solutions cannot simply be copied from cities like those in Japan without understanding local implications, Ghosh explains.    IMD forecasts and satellite tracking feed into a chain of over 800 multipurpose cyclone shelters and watchtowers across 120-plus coastal locations, from where sirens and mass alerts reach nearly 1,200 villages down to the last mile.   Early warning, meanwhile, can save lives immediately. "I would rather stress that we should have a very good early warning system. This is what I always tell," he says.  "With early warning, we can save a lot of people by making quick decisions," pointing to Cyclone Dana's 2024 forecast-driven school closures as an example. He calls this kind of forecasting work a silent scientific revolution, one that has quietly saved tens of thousands of lives without much public recognition. A blueprint that other states have borrowed Odisha's approach has not stayed confined to its coastline.  Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal have built similar community-based disaster preparedness and early warning frameworks, and the World Bank-backed National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project has extended comparable shelters, evacuation infrastructure, and warning systems across ten coastal states since 2010.    A dedicated IIT Bombay–BMC working group shares real-time monsoon data.   Community-based disaster preparedness manuals developed in Odisha were translated for wider circulation specifically so other states could adapt them. Researchers now regularly cite the "Odisha model" as a benchmark against which other coastal states measure their own preparedness. Mumbai's own experiment IIT Bombay has already built mumbaiflood.in, a portal offering a three-day rainfall forecast, a 90-minute radar-based nowcast, and a continuously updated flood inundation model, which received over 10,000 visits within days of launch.  A dedicated IIT Bombay–BMC working group shares this data in real time, and Ghosh describes the civic body's response as prompt, citing pump operations adjusted based on the institute's forecasts.  A new crowdsourced flood-reporting feature now adds ground-truth data from citizens to the model, and Ghosh believes Mumbai needs the same last-mile relay Odisha uses, since "not everyone can have access to internet, but at least a few people will have access, and they can immediately inform others." As Odisha's mangrove replanting drives show, resilience is often built through unglamorous, sustained science rather than singular fixes. Odisha's cyclone story suggests India already has a working model. The task now, experts say, is fine-tuning it for a flooding megacity. All images courtesy of TNIE Sources: ' Cyclone Biparjoy: IAS Officer Who Led Odisha's Stellar Disaster Management' : by The Better India, Published on 13 June 2023 ' Saving Over 1 Million Lives: How Odisha Saw Cyclone Fani in The Eye & Came Out Strong ': by The Better India, Published on 6 May 2019 ' Odisha's turnaround in disaster management has lessons for the world ': by The World Bank, Published on 3 November 2023 ' What states can learn from Odisha in disaster preparedness and mitigation ': by ReliefWeb/World Bank, Published on 14 June 2019 ' The "Odisha model" for disaster resilience ': by Ideas for India, Published on 16 August 2024

From Banana Leaf Meals to Fibre Bags: 10 Ways to Use Every Part of the Banana Plant
stories.summary: 1 Plant, 100 Uses explores the many ways familiar Indian plants, leaves, fruits and trees have been part of everyday life — from food and farming to homes, traditions and natural remedies. Each story takes one plant and uncovers the surprising ways people have found it useful, often across generations. In many Indian homes, the banana plant is a familiar sight . People buy its fruit at local markets, and they use its leaves during festivals and family gatherings. But the plant has uses that go well beyond what most people see in their kitchens.  Farmers and artisans have found ways to use parts usually left behind after harvest. Some have been part of Indian food traditions for generations, while others are helping turn farm waste into useful products. Here are a few ways the banana plant is used across India. 1. Ripe bananas make an easy snack Bananas are eaten across India as a snack or alongside breakfast. They are easy to carry and can be eaten without cooking once ripe.   Farmers and artisans have found ways to use parts usually left behind after harvest. Photograph: (Image generated by AI) The fruit is also used to make products that last longer than fresh bananas. The  ICAR National Research Centre for Banana documents the processing of bananas into products such as juice and banana fig. Banana pulp can also be used in jams and other preparations. 2. Raw bananas are a kitchen staple Raw bananas are cooked in homes across India. They are added to curries and dry vegetable dishes and are used in fried snacks. In Kerala, raw bananas are used to make the much-loved banana chips. The Nendran variety is particularly popular for this purpose. Raw bananas can also be dried and milled into flour for use in different food products. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research has documented ways to process bananas into products with a longer shelf life. Such methods can help reduce losses when fresh produce cannot be sold or consumed in time. 3. The banana flower is cooked as a vegetable The purple flower that hangs beneath a bunch of bananas is used in several regional cuisines. Once the outer bracts are removed, the small florets can be cleaned and cooked in curries and stir-fries. Banana flower dishes are found in parts of southern and eastern India. The flower can also be made into pickles. The ICAR National Research Centre for Banana has documented banana flower pickle as a value-added product. Preparing the flower takes time because the florets need to be cleaned individually. But in households where it is a familiar ingredient, this is normally part of cooking with the plant. 4. The tender inner stem is eaten The part commonly called the banana stem is actually a pseudostem made up of tightly packed leaf sheaths. At its centre is a tender core that is used in cooking.   In many Indian homes, the banana plant is a familiar sight. Photograph: (Image generated by AI) In southern Indian kitchens, the core is chopped and cooked as a vegetable. It is also used in juices and other preparations. The ICAR National Research Centre for Banana has documented products such as candy and pickles made from the central core. Using the inner core for food gives households another way to make use of the plant after its fruit has been harvested. 5. Banana leaves are used to serve food A meal served on a banana leaf is a familiar sight in many parts of southern India. The broad leaf holds rice and several accompaniments and is widely used during weddings and festivals. Banana leaves are also used to wrap certain foods and serve meals at community gatherings. Their size makes them convenient for serving a complete meal on one surface. The leaves have a place in traditional food practices as well as in everyday hospitality. Their use varies by region and occasion. 6. The pseudostem is turned into fibre After the banana bunch is harvested, the pseudostem is cut down. Instead of leaving all this material unused, farmers and entrepreneurs can process it to extract natural fibre. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research has documented banana fibre processing technology and its transfer to an entrepreneur in Uttar Pradesh. The fibre can be used to make ropes and garments as well as mats and carpets. Bags and baskets are other possible products. Processing the pseudostem requires equipment and suitable facilities. Where these are available, the material can become a source of raw material for small businesses. 7. Banana fibre is used in handicrafts The fibre extracted from banana plant material can be used to make items such as table mats and cushion covers. These products offer another use for material left behind after harvesting. In January 2024, the ICAR National Research Centre for Banana organised a training programme in Tamil Nadu on banana fibre craft and value addition. The programme aimed to help women learn skills that could be used to make products from banana sheath and its by-products. The ICAR report on the programme describes the initiative and its focus on developing craft skills. For those with access to training and buyers, such work can provide an additional source of income.   In Kerala, raw bananas are used to make the much-loved banana chips. Photograph: (PlotMyGarden) 8. Banana peels need not go straight into the bin Banana peels are usually discarded once the fruit has been eaten. Yet they can be put to use in food processing and composting. The ICAR National Research Centre for Banana has documented banana peel pickle as one way of using this part of the fruit. At home, the peels can be chopped and added to a compost bin along with other kitchen scraps and dry material. As the organic matter breaks down, it becomes part of the compost. This is a practical option for households that grow plants or maintain a garden. 9. Banana plants are used during ceremonies Banana plants are commonly used to decorate entrances and ceremonial spaces during weddings and religious occasions in several parts of India. Their green leaves and upright pseudostems are a familiar part of these arrangements. The plant is associated with auspicious occasions in many communities. The exact customs differ across regions, but banana plants continue to feature in traditional celebrations . Their role during these occasions is distinct from their use as food or raw material. They are part of the way families mark important events. 10. Banana residue can be used on farms Harvesting bananas leaves behind considerable plant material. The pseudostem and other suitable residues can be considered for composting or other forms of farm use rather than being discarded without thought. Research published through the Indian Council of Agricultural Research discusses banana plant parts and their place in integrated farming systems. The best use depends on the farm and the resources available. Some growers may be able to supply material to fibre processors while others may find composting more practical.   The fibre extracted from banana plant material can be used to make items such as table mats and cushion covers. Photograph: (Bunnings) Making use of what remains The banana plant serves different purposes in different parts of India. Its fruit and flower are cooked in homes while its leaves are used for serving food. These uses also offer farmers and small businesses ways to get more value from a crop . With suitable processing and local demand, parts of the plant that are left behind can become useful materials.

stories.title: ‘The Key Is Ensuring the Soil Doesn’t Retain Too Much Water’: 6 Tips to Grow Marigolds at Home
stories.summary: Few flowers can brighten a home garden like marigolds. Their cheerful yellow and orange blooms bring colour to balconies, terraces, and window ledges. They are also a familiar sight during Indian festivals, when they find their way into garlands and decorations. Growing them at home does not require a large garden, but it helps to understand what these flowers need to survive. From choosing the right variety to guaranteeing proper drainage, some useful lessons can be learnt from a farmer who has spent years cultivating marigolds. October and November are good months to grow marigolds in many parts of India, as the cooler weather can support their growth and flowering. If you are planning to add these cheerful blooms to your home garden, this is a good time to get started. Arup Kumar Ghosh, a farmer from Kolaghat in West Bengal’s East Midnapore district, began his journey in floriculture in 2011. After working at a flower shop in Hyderabad, he returned to his hometown and decided to cultivate marigolds himself. His first attempt was not successful. The local saplings he bought produced small flowers that did not meet market standards, resulting in losses. Determined to improve their quality, he travelled to Thailand and spent six months training at the Bangkok Blossom Market. There, he learnt about the Tennis Ball marigold variety, prized for its bright, round flowers. He brought back seeds of the yellow and orange varieties and began cultivating them on leased land. Reflecting on his early experiments, he told The Better India, “In the early stages of farming, I had to experiment with different fertilisers and treatments to find what worked best. It was all trial and error.” Over time, he developed his cultivation practices and expanded his farm. His experience offers several useful lessons for anyone looking to grow marigolds at home. 1. Give your marigolds plenty of sunlight Sunlight is one of the first things to consider when deciding where to grow marigolds. A shaded corner may not be the best place for these flowering plants.   October and November are good months to grow marigolds in many parts of India. Arup explains, “Marigolds need plenty of sunlight, so I make sure the land is not overshadowed by tall trees or other obstacles.” For home gardeners, this means choosing a sunny spot on a balcony, terrace, or in the garden. Place your pots where the plants can receive several hours of direct sunlight each day. If possible, avoid locations where taller plants or walls block the light for most of the day. 2. Choose your seeds and variety carefully Arup learnt the importance of choosing the right planting material through experience. The local marigold saplings he initially purchased produced small flowers that were not suitable for his business. During his training in Thailand, he discovered a new variety. He explains, “I learnt about a high-quality flower called the Tennis Ball marigold variety. This is prized for its bright, round flowers and its ability to withstand long-distance shipping without being damaged.” For a home garden, you can choose marigold seeds or saplings from a reliable nursery. Consider the space available, the colour you prefer, and the size of the flowers you want to grow. If you are new to gardening, starting with healthy saplings may be easier than raising plants from seeds. Check the leaves and stems before buying them, and avoid plants that appear diseased or badly damaged. 3. Make sure the soil drains well Water management has been an important part of Arup’s farming experience, particularly during the monsoon. “The key is ensuring the fields don’t retain too much water, especially during the monsoon,” he says. “I have to ensure the drainage system is effective, so the water doesn’t stagnate and harm the plants.” The same principle applies to marigolds grown in pots. Choose containers with drainage holes and use a potting mix that allows excess water to escape. Do not leave pots standing in water collected in trays.   Pests can affect flowering plants in home gardens as well as commercial farms. Photograph: (Bishy Barnabee's) Check the soil before watering. If it is still moist, wait before adding more water. The aim is to provide enough moisture for healthy growth without leaving the roots sitting in waterlogged soil. 4. Keep an eye out for pests Pests can affect flowering plants in home gardens as well as commercial farms. Regularly checking your marigolds can help you spot problems before they spread. The farmer shares his approach to managing pests, saying, “Instead of relying on harmful chemicals, I use neem oil, bone dust, and cow dung manure.” For home gardeners, it is important to understand that these materials serve different purposes. Neem oil products may help manage certain pests when used according to the label instructions. Bone dust and cow dung manure are soil amendments, not direct substitutes for pest control. Inspect the leaves and stems regularly for insects or unusual changes. If you use manure, make sure it is well-rotted and suitable for gardening. Use any fertiliser or soil amendment in the recommended quantity. 5. Take precautions during heavy rain  Unpredictable weather can damage marigold crops, particularly when heavy rain causes water to collect around the roots. Arup explains, “I cover the field with a net so they can grow well during harsh weather conditions.” A home garden will have different needs from a commercial farm, but a few easy precautions can still help. Move small pots to a sheltered area when strong winds or heavy rain are forecast. Secure taller plants so that they do not topple over, and make sure the drainage holes remain clear.   Sunlight is one of the first things to consider when deciding where to grow marigolds. Photograph: (Gardening Know How) After heavy rain, check your pots for standing water and allow excess moisture to drain away. 6. Be patient and learn from experience The farmer’s journey was not without setbacks. His first crop did not produce the quality he wanted, and he had to experiment with different methods before finding what worked for him. Home gardeners can take a similar approach by observing their plants and making adjustments when necessary. If your marigolds are not healthy, check whether they receive enough sunlight, whether the soil drains properly, and whether there are signs of pests. Use a fertiliser suitable for flowering plants and follow the recommended dosage. Avoid making several changes at once, as this can make it harder to understand what is helping or harming the plant.   Arup learnt the importance of choosing the right planting material through experience. Photograph: (Flowers Guide) Growing marigolds at home Arup Kumar Ghosh’s experience shows how observation, experimentation, and patience can help improve marigold cultivation. While growing flowers in a few pots is different from managing a commercial farm, the basics remain relevant. With the right growing conditions and consistent care, marigolds can bring a welcome splash of colour to your home garden. TBI Gardening Calendar brings together what to plant, grow, and care for each month of the year, helping home gardeners make the most of their balconies, terraces, backyards, and small growing spaces. Each story focuses on seasonal plants and crops, with simple, practical guidance on when to sow or plant, how to care for them, and what to expect as they grow.
