Snakebite Deaths in Odisha’s Angul Fell From 100+ to Double Digits. This Rescuer Is Changing How People Respond to Snakes
stories.summary: It is late in the evening on the outskirts of a village in Angul, Odisha. The green around them is dense, the road has given way to fields, and somewhere nearby, a snake has left people unsure of what to do next. The villagers keep their distance. However, the rescuers don't. They arrive with their hooks, bags, and equipment, first trying to identify the snake and then figuring out the safest way to get it out. Once it is secured, the team will coordinate with the Forest Department and release it in a suitable forested area. For Biplab Mahapatra, this is an ordinary rescue call. More than a decade ago, however, his life looked very different . He was a journalist, spending his days chasing stories. Today, he spends them chasing rescue calls, training volunteers and trying to convince people that the snake they fear does not necessarily have to be killed. One python rescue in 2011 inspired Biplab to build an organisation protecting wildlife in Odisha’s Angul district. "I have not chosen this job," he says. "It is destiny; this thing has chosen me." And his story of becoming a rescuer began with a python. From reporting stories to rescuing animals Biplab had always been drawn to nature . A professional climber, he spent years trekking and travelling through forests, including in Himachal Pradesh. He had also grown up around animals. His father, who was a journalist himself, was fond of pets, so their home often had Indian dogs. But journalism was still Biplab's profession. He was freelancing and working as a crime reporter when his interest in animal rescue began taking a more serious turn. He remembers rescuing dogs in those early days, but snakes had always fascinated him. Then came a large python that people were preparing to kill. The snake had eaten one of their goats. For the people who had lost their livestock, it was a threat that needed to be removed. From snakes to birds and civet cats, Rangers works to protect wildlife and reduce human-animal conflict. For Biplab, it was an animal that needed to be rescued. "I started with one rescue of a big, huge python," he recalls. "That inspired me to start a new organisation." The rescue also made him think about something much bigger happening around him. Angul had a serious human-wildlife conflict problem. Elephants, crocodiles and other animals regularly came into conflict with people, but Biplab noticed that there was little attention being paid to snakes. "There was no one to mitigate this thing in my place," he says. So, in 2011, he began working with People for Animals and started building what would eventually become People for Animals, Angul. In 2013, the organisation was formally registered. Biplab started it with three others, including a senior and two friends from different professions. For the first two years, he tried to balance the work with his career. Then he decided he couldn't do both. “I registered my organisation and started focusing on rescue full-time," he says. There was no big office or ready-made infrastructure waiting for him. In the early days, even keeping things running was a struggle. Through awareness sessions in schools, Biplab teaches children how to identify snakes, respond safely to encounters.   "Initially, funds were a big challenge for us. We were managing things with great difficulty," he says.  Even a snake rescue requires equipment such as hooks, bags, and other protective gear. But Biplab soon realised that equipment wasn't the only thing missing. There was something else the community needed: knowledge. 'The rescue is not the solution' At first, Biplab thought the answer was simple. A snake was in trouble, so he would rescue it. But the more calls he received, the more he understood the problem. There would always be another snake, a frightened family who had no idea whether the snake in front of them was venomous or harmless. "The rescue is not the solution ," Biplab says. That realisation changed the organisation's work. Instead of only responding to rescue calls, Biplab began taking the conversation to schools, colleges and villages. He developed an awareness programme called Save Snakes, Save Humans , teaching people how to identify snakes, respond to encounters and understand snakebite first aid. A major part of the work was addressing myths. Through Save Snakes, Save Humans, Rangers teaches communities to replace fear with knowledge and respond safely to snakes. Biplab has heard plenty over the years: that snakes can capture photographs with their eyes, that they love drinking milk, that a nag-nagin pair takes revenge, or that snakes carry money in their heads. He laughs at some of the ideas but knows that the consequences of misinformation can be serious. "I feel that when there is a lack of knowledge, it is always dangerous," he says. "When people don't know about this beautiful creature, they see it as a threat." And fear, in turn, can lead to killing. Biplab believes that the problem goes far beyond Odisha. Snakebite is a major public health concern across India, with thousands of people losing their lives every year. What makes it worse, he says, is that many cases are not even properly reported. His solution is not to tell people not to be afraid. It is to give them enough knowledge to know what to do with that fear. When the phone rings, someone has to go Today, the organisation, now known as Rangers, has around 50 volunteers in Angul, with more than 30 actively involved. Its network extends across Odisha and into other parts of India. When a rescue call comes in, the first thing the team does is assess the situation. Can the caller identify the snake? If not, Biplab's advice is simple: stay away, keep a safe distance, and, if possible, keep an eye on where the snake is. If it has entered a room, the safest option may be to close the room and wait for a trained rescuer. Then comes the race against distance. Angul is geographically large, so Rangers have volunteers spread across different parts of the district. Whoever is closest to the location takes the call. Once there, the rescuer identifies the snake and follows the protocol for that particular species. After the animal is safely rescued, the team informs the Forest Department and releases it in the nearest suitable forest. On paper, it sounds straightforward, but on the ground things are different.  Biplab remembers one call that came from the Forest Department at around 9.30 pm. A large snake had fallen into an abandoned well. The well was nearly 30 feet deep. The location was about 80 kilometres away. Once they reached the area, the team had to leave the motorable road, walk through paddy fields and then continue towards a forest reserve. Rangers volunteers rescue snakes and coordinate with the Forest Department to release them in suitable habitats. They had no proper way to get into the well. "So I just told them to arrange a ladder and some rope," Biplab recalls. "I was the man who went first." Only after reaching the bottom did they realise how big the python was. And then it wrapped itself around his arm. "It almost choked me from my left hand," he says. "It was already wrapped around me fully from my wrist to my shoulder." Biplab struggled to breathe as the snake tightened its grip. His senior and volunteers helped him get free. The python was eventually rescued and released in the nearest forest. It turned out to be about 15 feet long; for Biplab, the lesson was simple. "Every rescue is a story," he says. Building people, not just a rescue team The biggest change in Biplab's work has perhaps been that he is no longer trying to do everything himself. He is building people who can respond when he isn't there. One of them is Manoj Vishwakarma, Biplab's childhood friend and the head of Rangers' domestic wing, which handles rescues involving dogs, cattle, and other domestic animals. Manoj had a completely different career. He worked in Bengaluru at Bosch and initially only supported Biplab from the sidelines. "I used to come and check with him, like what he is doing," Manoj recalls. "I saw some snakes he used to capture and always used to get scared of them.” During the work-from-home period after COVID, Manoj got an opportunity to spend more time helping. Gradually, the occasional calls became regular involvement. He remembers one incident when he was in Bihar and came across an injured nilgai. Instead of wondering what to do, he called Biplab, who helped connect him with the local Forest Department. For Manoj, it showed him that helping an animal didn't always require some extraordinary intervention. Sometimes, it started with knowing whom to call. He eventually left his job and began working full-time with Rangers. For Biplab, success lies not just in rescuing animals, but in helping communities respond without fear or violence. "People look at you like a saviour. Like you have saved something and helped them." For him, that feeling is very different from a conventional workday. Rangers has two broad wings, one focused on domestic animals and another on wildlife. Besides snakes, its volunteers rescue monkeys, civet cats, turtles, monitor lizards and birds. Biplab doesn't insist on a particular educational qualification when selecting volunteers. "He must be passionate," he says. Training and monitoring then follow. Volunteers are taught rescue protocols, and the team tracks details such as where an animal was rescued and where it was released through geotagging. The aim is to make sure that the rescue is safe for everyone involved. Changing what happens after people see a snake For Biplab, the real impact of the work is not just the number of snakes rescued, but what happens before his team even arrives. According to district medical data he cites, snakebite deaths in Angul, which once crossed 100 annually, have fallen to double digits over the past five years. The organisation has also taken its awareness programmes to around 40 to 50 schools, helping children and communities understand that a snake does not have to be killed simply because it enters their space. Manoj has seen that shift himself. "Don't kill because they're in the food chain," he says. "They have their own responsibilities. Those animals are required." With around 50 volunteers in Angul, Rangers is building a network to respond to wildlife rescue calls across the district. For Biplab, that is the larger goal. "There are so many cases where we have to choose people's safety first," he says. "Only saving animals is not our mission. Our mission is to balance between [humans and wildlife]. And our main mission is coexistence." His work has since expanded beyond rescue calls. He has volunteered with the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau on wildlife trafficking cases and worked with the Odisha Forest Department on conservation awareness. His work has earned two Limca Book of Records entries and a world record, while a 12-minute snake awareness film received national recognition, finishing as second runner-up in the short-film category under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. But recognition has never made the work less dangerous. Fear never really leaves Biplab was once bitten by a highly venomous banded krait and spent five days in an ICU in Cuttack after being taken through multiple hospitals. There, he saw how many snakebite patients had delayed proper treatment after first turning to faith healers. He has also faced danger while working against wildlife crime. While helping catch poachers involved in the killing of a spotted deer, his team was shot at. In another case involving an elephant killed for its tusks, they again came under fire. So, is he afraid? "Yes. Whoever says he is not afraid, he is a fool," he says. Fear, he admits, never really leaves. But neither does the work. Now, his biggest dream is to build a community that can continue without him. "For me, this is not about Biplab Mahapatra. This is about these 50 other people who have dedicated their life, their sweat, their blood for this thing." Because there will always be another rescue call, another frightened villager, and another animal that needs help. The hope is that, one day, there will also be enough people who know exactly what to do. All images courtesy of Biplab Mahapatra

stories.title: Why Kashmir’s Chinar Trees Turn Fiery Red Every Autumn While Many Indian Trees Stay Green
stories.summary: Every October, something beautiful begins to happen across Kashmir. The broad green leaves of the chinar trees slowly turn yellow. Soon, shades of orange and red begin to appear. By November, entire trees seem to glow in the autumn sunlight, their branches covered in leaves ranging from golden yellow to deep crimson. For Kashmiris, this is a familiar sign that winter is approaching. Known locally as boen or buen , the chinar ( Platanus orientalis ) is Jammu and Kashmir's state tree. Its enormous canopy provides shade through summer, while its changing colours have become one of the Valley's most recognisable autumn sights. But have you ever wondered why chinars turn such beautiful shades of red while so many trees in warmer parts of India stay green? The answer begins inside a single leaf. What happens to a leaf when winter approaches? Throughout spring and summer, chinar leaves are busy making food for the tree. Their green colour comes from chlorophyll, a natural substance that helps leaves absorb sunlight. Using this energy, the leaves turn water and carbon dioxide into sugars that help the tree grow. But as autumn arrives, Kashmir's days become shorter and temperatures begin to fall. The tree senses that winter is approaching and starts preparing for the colder months. Girls walk in a garden covered with fallen Chinar leaves during the autumn season in Kashmir https://t.co/byT5eUWu2C — Basit Zargar (باسط) (@basiitzargar) November 27, 2021 Before shedding its leaves, it draws back useful nutrients that can be stored and used again when spring arrives. As this happens, the green chlorophyll gradually breaks down. And something fascinating follows. Colours that were hidden beneath the green begin to appear. In their February 2011 Science Reporter article, Fiery Chinar , researchers Mohammad Imran Kozgar and Samiullah Khan explain how falling temperatures and declining chlorophyll reveal two groups of pigments called carotenes and xanthophylls. These are responsible for yellow and orange shades. In simple terms, the colours were already present in the leaves. The green was simply hiding them. But where does that beautiful red come from? Red leaves have another interesting story. In many trees that change colour during autumn, red and purple shades come from pigments called anthocyanins. Unlike the yellow and orange pigments, these can be produced as autumn progresses. Their formation is influenced by sunlight, temperature and the amount of sugar present in the leaves. However, scientists have not established exactly which pigments produce every shade of crimson seen in Kashmir's chinars. The 2011 article specifically explains the appearance of yellow and orange pigments. Kashmir's climate plays an important role in this seasonal transformation. Its broad canopy, distinctive leaves and striking autumn colours have made it a defining feature of the Valley’s landscape. Photograph: (News18/Bashir Lone ; Getty Images)   Chinars are deciduous trees, meaning they shed their leaves before winter. The Valley's shorter autumn days and falling temperatures help trigger this process. In warmer parts of India, many trees follow different seasonal patterns. Some remain green throughout the year, while others shed leaves during the dry season. For chinars, the changing colours mark a natural process of preparing for winter and conserving resources for the next growing season. Why Kashmir is working to save these trees The chinar's place in Kashmir extends far beyond its autumn colours. Mughal rulers planted these trees across the Valley, including at Srinagar's famous Naseem Bagh near Dal Lake. Their distinctive leaves continue to appear in Kashmiri embroidery, carpets and papier-mâché. But the trees have faced threats from damage, neglect and unauthorised cutting. In January 2025, The Indian Express reported on Jammu and Kashmir's Tree Aadhaar initiative, which gives individual chinars a unique identity to help authorities protect them. Project coordinator Dr Syed Tariq said that 28,560 trees had been geo-tagged at the time. Their records include location, age, size, health and possible threats, helping authorities keep track of individual trees. As Kashmir's chinars prepare to shed their leaves each winter, efforts to protect them carry a simple hope: that future generations will still be able to walk beneath their shade in summer and watch their leaves turn gold and crimson every autumn. Sources: ‘Geo-tagging and ‘Aadhaar’: How, why the J&K govt is trying to conserve chinar trees’ : Bashaarat Masood, Published on 26 January 2025 ‘Fiery Chinar’ : By Mohd. Imran Kozgar and Samiullah Khan, Published in February 2011

stories.title: ‘People Saw Her Diagnosis Before They Saw Her’: How a Mother Built a Platform for Artists With Disabilities
stories.summary: A paintbrush moves slowly across the paper. Dhriti is focused on the colours in front of her, adding one shade after another to a painting that, to someone else, may simply look like a piece of art. But to her mother, Shweta Runwal, moments like these hold a much deeper meaning. Years ago, when Dhriti was still a little girl and could speak only in single words, she came home with a diary. On one of its pages, she had drawn two stick figures. One of them was crying. Shweta was worried and asked her daughter what had happened. Dhriti tried to explain that her friend was moving away. “It was the first time I realised she was actually trying to communicate through art,” Shweta recalls. For a mother who had spent years hearing questions about what her daughter would or would not be able to do, the moment offered a different possibility. Perhaps the better question was not what Dhriti could not do, but what she could express, create and become. From paintings to lifestyle products, Tickle Your Art brings original artwork by neurodiverse artists to a wider audience while preserving the individuality of their work. That question would eventually grow into Tickle Your Art, a social enterprise that works with artists with Down syndrome and intellectual disabilities, turning their original artwork into lifestyle products, books, corporate gifts and more. But the idea did not begin as a business. It began at home, with Dhriti. Before the diagnosis, there was Dhriti  Dhriti was diagnosed with Down syndrome a few days after she was born. At two months, doctors also discovered a hole in her heart and advised the family to consider surgery. For Shweta, the early years came with another challenge: the assumptions surrounding her daughter's diagnosis. “People saw her diagnosis before they saw her,” she says. “They had already written her off.” There were questions about whether Dhriti would walk or talk, whether she would ever have a career, and what her future would look like. At the time, Shweta says, there were fewer avenues for parents to find information or connect. Dhriti was Tickle Your Art’s first artist. Today, the social enterprise has worked with more than 25 neurodiverse artists. Her own parents, however, took a different approach. “They were like, ‘Just treat her like any other baby,” she recalls. That trust became Shweta's biggest support system. She had trained as an architect and had also worked in London, where she first discovered how powerfully art and design could be used as forms of expression. But as Dhriti grew, Shweta began volunteering with the Down Syndrome Federation of India and meeting more families. She slowly began to notice a gap. The conversation was often about what children with intellectual disabilities might not be able to do. Shweta wanted to ask a different question: What if we started with what they could? Art became a language and a possibility After Dhriti's early experience with drawing, Shweta began looking for art classes for her. She eventually started working with several children, helping them explore different forms of creative expression. For Shweta, inclusion begins by looking beyond a diagnosis and recognising the creativity, skills and possibilities each person brings. In 2018, she organised an exhibition at Kelkar Museum around World Down Syndrome Day, bringing together artwork by people with Down syndrome and creating products around it. The response stayed with her. What began as a personal experiment eventually became Tickle Your Art, which was formally registered in October 2020, during the pandemic. Dhriti became its very first artist. Within six months, more artists began joining; today, Tickle Your Art has worked with more than 25 neurodiverse artists and is onboarding six more for upcoming launches.  The organisation also runs a community centre where artists receive training, mentorship and employment opportunities, alongside an experience centre where visitors can encounter their work and the stories behind it. Importantly, the artists do not have to fit into a predetermined idea of what “good” art should look like. “We try not to change the artwork as much as possible,” says Shweta. “We want to see their story.” Dhriti’s artwork was first showcased at an exhibition organised by Shweta at Kelkar Museum in 2018. Sometimes, that means designing around an artist's original lines or colours. Sometimes, it means finding a new way to translate their work into a product. Every product carries the story of its artist. Shweta describes the idea simply: each product should be responsible for “three smiles” — that of the artist, the person giving it and the person receiving it. At home, inclusion came naturally  For Ira, Shweta's younger daughter, this entire world has always been normal. “I've never felt this is very different,” Ira says. “I've never thought about inclusion, because it is normal for me, and that's how it should be for everyone.” That belief has grown alongside the enterprise. Today, Ira contributes to Tickle Your Art's marketing and design decisions. Shweta jokes that nothing goes into production without Ira's approval. Ira can look at a product and instinctively understand what might appeal to someone, where something should be placed, or how a design could work better. Ira Runwal contributes to Tickle Your Art’s marketing and design, believing inclusion should be a natural part of everyday life. But her role goes beyond the business. She also speaks about inclusion in schools and has received recognition for doing so. For Shweta, watching her daughters grow up together has reinforced something she has long believed: inclusion does not have to be complicated. “It doesn't belong to anybody,” she says. “Just give a smile, and others will smile back at you.” When talent finds a place to work  For Shweta, economic inclusion is not simply about giving someone a job. It is about helping them recognise that their time, talent and contribution have value. She remembers when Rohan, a 33-year-old artist with a background in animation and digital design, began working with Tickle Your Art. When Shweta started paying him, his father wondered whether the small organisation should really be giving him a salary. For Shweta, there was no question.“He is giving his time. He is coming here sincerely. And I feel that needs to add value,” she says. That philosophy is also reflected in the way Tickle Your Art operates. Artists can work from home or at the centre, and their work is developed into products based on its originality and the story behind it. The organisation has now worked with artists across India, with many connections coming through disability organisations and communities. At Tickle Your Art, Rohan has found an opportunity to reconnect with his passion for art and rebuild his confidence through meaningful work. For Suzanne, who brings around three decades of HR experience and works with Tickle Your Art as an HR consultant, this has also changed the way she understands inclusion. “In corporate, we talk about diversity, equity and inclusion,” she says. “But very rarely do we get to live it the way Shweta is living it.” Her role is largely focused on building the systems and processes that allow the organisation to function sustainably, while Shweta works closely with the artists and creative side. Suzanne says she has also noticed something else: people sometimes hesitate because they do not know how to interact with people with intellectual disabilities. “But I have found Dhriti to be extremely loving, warm, intelligent and funny,” she says. “They are just like you and I. There's no difference.” When confidence finds its way back  Before Tickle Your Art, 33-year-old Rohan had already worked in animation and had trained in Photoshop, Illustrator and other digital tools. But after his earlier job ended during the lockdown, he became more introverted. Then came Tickle Your Art; Rohan has now been associated with the organisation for around a year. His mother, Veena, says art has always been one of his biggest interests. At Tickle Your Art, however, she has watched that interest become a source of confidence and happiness again. Tickle Your Art develops products around artists’ original creations, ensuring their distinctive styles and stories remain at the heart of the process. For Veena, that happiness is perhaps the most meaningful change. She has also seen how spaces like Tickle Your Art can shift the conversation for families, giving children opportunities to learn, work and meet people outside their homes. And that, ultimately, is what Shweta wants to build. A space that feels like home Tickle Your Art has received recognition from several platforms, including Shark Tank India, where Anupam Mittal invested in the venture. It has also received grant support from Jeet Adani, been recognised as an “Industry Disruptor” by UN Women, and showcased its work internationally in Berlin at The DO and H&M exhibition. Dhriti, meanwhile, received the National Award for Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities in the Shreshth Divyang Balika category for her achievements in art and her role in promoting inclusion. For Shweta, these milestones matter, but not simply because they validate the organisation. She remembers a parent of a six-month-old child with Down syndrome reaching out after seeing Dhriti's videos. The mother told her that she had felt shattered after the diagnosis, but seeing Dhriti had given her hope. “That is what makes me feel that all of this is worth it,” Shweta says. Dhriti received the National Award for her achievements in art and contribution to promoting inclusion. Her dream now is to build similar community spaces across India, places where families can come together, where artists can learn and work, and where art can become a bridge to meaningful livelihoods. Ira imagines Tickle Your Art becoming known across India and eventually the world. Shweta has an even simpler measure of success: working with many more artists and giving them a platform to begin. For her, the centre should feel like a second home. A place where a person's diagnosis does not decide their possibilities, where a painting is not treated as something made “despite” a disability, but simply as someone's art. And perhaps, most importantly, a place where inclusion stops being a lofty idea and becomes what Ira has always known it to be — normal. All images courtesy of Shweta Runwal

stories.title: ‘This Is the Horse From My Book’: How a Farm Visit Brought Animals to Life for a Toddler
stories.summary: This story is part of “Parenting: What Google Won’t Tell You” — The Better India’s people-led parenting series that goes beyond conventional advice to document how real families are actually raising their children. Through real parents, parenting coaches, influencers and experts, the series brings honest, diverse and relatable perspectives on the questions, choices, challenges and solutions that shape everyday parenting — the things Google can’t always answer. When Aayansh Singh first visited a farm near Mumbai, the horses, pigs and hens he had seen in picture books suddenly had a life of their own. Two years later, he returned with one wish: to ride a horse. For his father, Bhanu Singh, a software engineer based in Mumbai, watching that wish come true was a reminder of how much a child can take away from an experience that seems simple to an adult. “When we first took him, I honestly thought he would forget everything because he was only two years old,” Bhanu recalls. “But for the next year, he kept talking about the horses and remembering the farm.” It began with a small observation at home. Aayansh, then two, could identify horses, pigs, cows and goats from his picture books. He knew what they looked like, but he had never encountered them outside the pages. What began as a day of discovery became a memory Aayansh continued to talk about long after returning home. “We wanted him to go beyond books and experience them firsthand, to see them up close, touch them, and understand how they feel and behave,” Bhanu says. That thought led the family to Japalouppe, a farm they discovered while searching online for a place near Mumbai where their toddler could meet animals. When the pictures came alive The family kept their first outing simple. Japalouppe was about a 1.5-hour drive away, making it manageable for a day trip with a young child . There was no packed itinerary or long list of attractions to tick off. For Bhanu Singh, the experience was a reminder that simple outings can leave lasting impressions on young children. Bhanu was drawn to the farm's open spaces, animals and horses. They also carried some food, unsure whether they would find suitable, non-spicy options for Aayansh. To their pleasant surprise, the farm had a child-friendly menu. Once they arrived, the family let the day unfold at Aayansh's pace. “He didn't run around shouting or get overwhelmed. He was quiet, curious, and busy taking everything in,” Bhanu remembers. One moment that stayed with him was watching his son run around the hens. Until then, hens had been pictures in a book. Now, they were moving around him, clucking and going about their business. The horses and pigs offered another kind of discovery. “He looked at the horse like he was thinking, ‘This is the horse from my book.’ He did the same with the pig. In his book, it was just a picture, but here it had a smell and made a sound. For him, it was a big thing.” The family’s two visits showed how hands-on experiences can help children build on what they learn from books. For the adults, these might have been ordinary sights and sounds. For Aayansh, they were details that no picture could quite capture. The family stayed close, letting him decide how near he wanted to get to each animal. A dedicated guide showed them how to approach and handle the animals safely, explaining which feed to offer and how to do it. There was no need to hurry him along. If something caught his attention, he could stay and watch. From watching horses to riding one The first visit was about getting acquainted with the animals. Aayansh was too young to ride a horse, but the experience left him with memories he continued to talk about long after the family returned home. Then, at three and a half, he asked to visit the farm again; this time, he had a plan of his own. “He clearly told us he wanted to visit again and ride a horse,” Bhanu says. At three and a half, Aayansh returned to the farm with a wish of his own: to ride a horse. The family returned, and Aayansh got his wish. He was the youngest child on the farm to ride a horse that day, making the moment especially memorable for his parents. Bhanu noticed how much had changed. On the first visit, his son had watched the animals with wide-eyed curiosity. Now, he knew what he wanted to do. He approached the experience with greater confidence , going around to meet the animals again, almost as if he were reconnecting with old friends. “For us, the most special part was watching him sit on the horse with so much pride,” Bhanu says. “The first trip was about discovery, while the second was about building on those memories and trying something new on his own.” A holiday doesn't need a packed itinerary The two visits changed the way Bhanu thinks about family holidays. Earlier, he associated a good holiday with travelling to a new destination and having plenty of activities planned. Now, he finds himself asking a different question before choosing a place: “What will my child actually experience here? What will he see, feel, and remember?” His advice to parents who want to introduce young children to nature is to start small. Choose a place close to home, perhaps somewhere connected to an animal or activity the child already loves, and leave room for curiosity to lead the way. “Don't try to fit too many activities into one day. Let your child explore at their own pace, follow their curiosity, and enjoy the little moments,” he says. After all, Aayansh's first farm visit wasn't filled with elaborate attractions or a faraway holiday backdrop. It was a day of watching hens, meeting pigs and standing close to horses he had previously known only from books. For parents, Aayansh’s story is a reminder that meaningful family holidays need not involve packed itineraries or faraway destinations. Yet those encounters stayed with him.  They even gave him something to look forward to when the family returned. stories.title: Jackfruit Peel Could Help Clean Water: NIT Rourkela Team Removes 90% of Harmful Fluoride
stories.summary: Cut open a ripe jackfruit, and you are greeted by its golden-yellow flesh, sweet aroma and sticky, fibrous peel. While the juicy fruit often finds its way into curries, chips and desserts, its thick outer covering usually ends up in the bin. Researchers at the National Institute of Technology (NIT) Rourkela , however, have found another use for this often-discarded part of the fruit. They have turned jackfruit peel into a material that removed more than 90% of fluoride from contaminated water in laboratory tests, in about 10 minutes. The idea brings together two things that rarely make it into the same conversation: fruit waste and safer drinking water. For families whose groundwater contains too much fluoride, which can damage teeth and bones over time, this innovation could eventually offer a more affordable way to make drinking water safer.  How does jackfruit peel help clean water? The secret lies in what researchers have made from the peel. The team converted discarded jackfruit peel into activated carbon and modified it with zirconium, a metal that helps the material capture fluoride from water. Modified with zirconium, jackfruit-peel-based activated carbon helps capture excess fluoride from contaminated water. Photograph: ( Nature ) Prof. Susmita Mishra, Professor in the Department of Chemical Engineering at NIT Rourkela, explains the thinking behind the innovation. “The key idea behind this technology is to use an agricultural waste material as a resource for water purification. We prepared activated carbon from discarded jackfruit peel and modified it with zirconium to improve its ability to capture fluoride from water,” she adds.  The material showed promising results in laboratory tests, removing over 90% of fluoride within approximately 10 minutes under the tested conditions. Fluoride occurs naturally in water, but drinking water containing too much of it over a long period can damage teeth and bones. This condition, known as fluorosis, can affect both children and adults.  Removing excess fluoride, however, is not always straightforward. Reverse osmosis, a widely used water treatment method, can waste considerable amounts of water and remove minerals such as calcium and magnesium. Other methods, including ion exchange and activated alumina, also come with limitations, including the use of chemicals that can raise environmental concerns. The NIT Rourkela team's approach explores whether an agricultural by-product can help make fluoride removal more accessible. What did the researchers find? In laboratory experiments, the jackfruit-peel-based material removed more than 90% of fluoride from water containing around 1–5 milligrams per litre. Under the tested conditions, the team recorded removal efficiencies of over 90–97% within 10–20 minutes. The patented innovation by NIT Rourkela researchers offers a new approach to tackling fluoride contamination using agricultural waste. Photograph: ( Gujarat Samachar ) The researchers have also secured a patent for the technology. The team comprises Prof. Mishra and Dr. Pratima Minz, Research Graduate at NIT Rourkela. They estimate that preparing the material costs approximately Rs 37 per gram, based on the electricity and chemicals used in its synthesis. These are promising early findings, but there is still some way to go before the material can be used to treat drinking water outside the laboratory. The research has reached Technology Readiness Level 4 (TRL 4), meaning the material and its underlying concept have been validated in a laboratory environment. What happens next? For families in rural and semi-urban areas where groundwater contains excess fluoride, an affordable treatment option could make a meaningful difference. The researchers hope their material could eventually be used in decentralised water treatment systems, bringing purification closer to the communities that need it. Prof. Mishra says, “The potential of this technology lies in its use of an easily available agricultural by-product to develop a cost-effective material for fluoride removal. In the long term, the technology could contribute to water treatment solutions for communities in fluoride-affected regions, subject to further testing and validation.” The team is now working towards a prototype to test the material’s potential beyond the laboratory. Photograph: ( The Printlines ) The next step is to develop a  physical prototype and test how the material performs in practical conditions. The team will also study its long-term performance and operating costs to understand whether it can be deployed on a larger scale. A discarded jackfruit peel is not yet ready to make drinking water safer on its own. But this research offers an interesting possibility: something routinely thrown away could, with further development, become part of a solution to a problem that affects communities across India.
